title: Concentrated ferrofluids stable against realistic contamination
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Formulate high-magnetization ferrofluids that retain particle dispersion, usable viscosity, and magnetic response after long storage, thermal excursions, and realistic water or chemical contamination. Establish quantitative compatibility rules for nanoparticles, coatings, and carrier fluids.
status: Colloidal stability has constrained ferrofluid design for decades. A 2025 ionic-liquid formulation improved stability and tunable anisotropy while identifying water contamination as a strong destabilizer; broad environmental qualification remains open.
why: Improves the lifetime of magnetic liquid seals, actuators, and separation systems.
key_works: Talone et al. (2025), “Novel Formulation of Ionic Liquid-Based Ferrofluids: Investigation of the Magnetic Properties,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.langmuir.5c00403).

title: Magnetorheological shelf stability without excessive off-state viscosity
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Prevent irreversible settling and hard sediment formation while preserving low zero-field viscosity, high field-induced yield stress, and rapid redispersion. Validate stored fluids inside operating devices as well as laboratory containers.
status: Coatings, particle-size mixtures, thixotropic additives, and mixing offer partial improvements. A 2025 analysis explores ultrasound–magnetic coupling, but competing stability, flow, and energy requirements remain formulation-dependent.
why: Enables reliable dampers, clutches, brakes, and haptic devices after long idle periods.
key_works: Palumbo and Versaci (2025), “Controlling Sedimentation in Magnetorheological Fluids Through Ultrasound–Magnetic Field Coupling: Multiscale Analysis and Applications,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3390/math13152540).

title: Predicting magnetorheological-fluid degradation in service
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Predict loss of yield stress and changes in drag, wear, and redispersibility under combined shear, heating, oxidation, and cycling. Establish accelerated tests that correctly rank service lifetime across formulations and geometries.
status: Commercial devices already exist. A 2025 braking study developed an accelerated durability bench representing 100,000 km; transfer to other thermal histories and contact conditions remains unresolved.
why: Replaces trial-and-error replacement with dependable lifetime engineering.
key_works: Imberti et al. (2025), “Durability Analysis of a Magneto-Rheological Fluid for Automotive Braking System,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3390/designs9030074).

title: Coupled Brownian, Néel, and collective relaxation in concentrated ferrofluids
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Develop predictive nonequilibrium models incorporating internal moment reversal, particle rotation, dipolar clustering, polydispersity, and hydrodynamic interactions. Reproduce magnetic response and flow under strong time-dependent fields without refitting each experiment.
status: Brownian and Néel mechanisms are established, and a 2024 model treats their coupled nonlinear response for individual particles. Concentrated interacting suspensions require additional collective physics.
why: Connects nanoparticle design to controllable macroscopic magnetic-fluid behavior.
key_works: Ilg (2024), “Nonequilibrium response of magnetic nanoparticles to time-varying magnetic fields: Contributions from Brownian and Néel processes,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.109.034603).

title: Nonlinear ferrofluid-interface failure in nonuniform fields
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Predict transitions from stable interfaces to spikes, jets, rupture, and droplet shedding under realistic gradients, imposed flow, and moving contact lines. Validate morphology and failure thresholds across immiscible fluid pairs.
status: The classical Rosensweig instability is understood in idealized settings. A 2024 study matched theory and experiments for water-based ferrofluids against air and oil; dynamic topology changes remain harder.
why: Enables controlled liquid patterning and prevents loss of magnetic-fluid barriers.
key_works: Li et al. (2024), “The Rosensweig instability at the interface between ferrofluids and immiscible fluids,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2023.171608).

title: Public run-to-failure data for ferrofluid seals
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Build an interoperable dataset linking geometry, formulation, operating history, vibration, temperature, leakage, and failure mechanisms. Include censored lifetimes and independent validation cases for remaining-life prediction.
status: Numerous component studies and successful seals exist. A 2026 reliability review identifies public run-to-failure data and experimentally validated prognostics as missing foundations.
why: Enables comparable reliability models and evidence-based maintenance.
key_works: Li, Si, Liu, Zhang, and Li (2026), “Intelligent Reliability of Ferrofluid Seals: A Review,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3390/act15080428).

title: Robust inverse design of load-bearing magnetic soft machines
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Jointly design geometry, magnetization, and material distribution for prescribed three-dimensional motion and force despite fabrication errors, aging, contact, and changing loads. Determine which trajectories are physically realizable with available fields.
status: A 2025 framework demonstrated joint morphology and magnetic-profile design. Reliable transfer to uncertain loading and manufacturing conditions remains open.
why: Turns demonstration-specific actuators into reusable design platforms.
key_works: Karacakol, Alapan, Demir, and Sitti (2025), “Data-driven design of shape-programmable magnetic soft materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58091-z).

title: Durable low-energy remagnetization during soft-machine operation
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Reprogram local magnetization repeatedly with small thermal excursions, low total energy, and minimal degradation of shape, force, and retained patterns. Scale independently addressable regions without excessive heating complexity.
status: Addressable in-situ reprogramming was demonstrated in 2025 using phase-change composites and frequency-selective heating. Long-cycle durability, energy optimization, and dense addressing remain distinct targets.
why: Lets one magnetic machine adapt its function during use.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), “Addressable and perceptible dynamic reprogram of ferromagnetic soft machines,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57454-w).

title: Scalable independent three-dimensional control of many magnetic robots
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Independently steer many nearby robots through three-dimensional trajectories while bounding cross-coupling, heating, field strength, and collisions. Determine how controllable degrees of freedom scale with actuator count and volume.
status: A 2025 coil-array system controlled up to 72 ferrofluid droplets. Planar achievements do not settle dense volumetric control under fixed power and hardware budgets.
why: Enables parallel micromanipulation and coordinated magnetic assembly.
key_works: Cui et al. (2025), “Development of an Electromagnetic Coil Array System for Large-Scale Ferrofluid Droplet Robots Programmable Control,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2025.3584430).

title: Transferable closed-loop control in unknown magnetic-robot environments
subfield: Ferrofluids, magnetorheological materials, and magnetic soft machines
open: Control robots reliably when geometry, friction, flow, visibility, and magnetic response differ from training conditions. Demonstrate disturbance recovery and calibrated failure detection without extensive retraining.
status: Reinforcement-learning-based autonomous three-dimensional positioning and planning were demonstrated in 2024. Generalization, partial observability, and cross-platform evaluation remain open.
why: Enables dependable operation in unstructured industrial and laboratory environments.
key_works: Abbasi et al. (2024), “Autonomous 3D positional control of a magnetic microrobot using reinforcement learning,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-023-00779-2).

title: Quantitative finite-temperature spin–lattice thermodynamics
open: Predict magnetic phase boundaries, magnetostriction, and thermal expansion with one coupled electronic–spin–lattice model whose parameters are independently validated across phases.
status: Atomistic spin–lattice dynamics has been practical since at least 2008. Accurate forces in one state do not ensure correct magnetic entropy, longitudinal fluctuations, or transition sampling.
why: Makes temperature-dependent materials design more reliable.
key_works: Ma, Woo, and Dudarev (2008), “Large-scale simulation of the spin-lattice dynamics in ferromagnetic iron,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.78.024434).

title: Reliable noncollinear magnetic ground-state discovery
open: Automatically find and verify ground states with long periods, noncollinearity, spin–orbit coupling, and competing distortions, reporting uncertainty when states are nearly degenerate.
status: High-throughput collinear enumeration and spin-informed models exist. They do not certify global minima over arbitrary magnetic periods and textures.
why: Prevents screening pipelines from assigning incorrect phases or rejecting useful compounds.
key_works: Horton et al. (2019), “High-throughput prediction of the ground-state collinear magnetic order of inorganic materials using Density Functional Theory,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-019-0199-7); Xu et al. (2025), “Spin-informed universal graph neural networks for simulating magnetic ordering,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422973122).

title: Transferable machine-learned magnetic potentials
open: Train spin-aware potentials that remain accurate for defects, surfaces, changed chemistry, noncollinear states, and phase transitions, with calibrated failure detection.
status: The 2025 spin-informed graph-network work improves magnetic-order ranking and electronic-structure initialization. Transfer to coupled finite-temperature spin and atomic dynamics remains a stronger requirement.
why: Enables large realistic simulations beyond direct electronic-structure calculations.
key_works: Xu et al. (2025), “Spin-informed universal graph neural networks for simulating magnetic ordering,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422973122); Ma et al. (2008), “Large-scale simulation of the spin-lattice dynamics in ferromagnetic iron,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.78.024434).

title: Magnetic lifetime prediction across inaccessible timescales
open: Predict years-long reversal probabilities from tractable simulations, including multiple pathways, entropy, disorder, and time-varying operating conditions.
status: Transition-state methods calculate barriers and prefactors for model spins. Extrapolation to defective devices remains difficult when dominant escape mechanisms change with temperature or field.
why: Connects microscopic dynamics to retention and reliability requirements.
key_works: Bessarab, Uzdin, and Jónsson (2012), “Harmonic transition-state theory of thermal spin transitions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.85.184409); Brown (1963), “Thermal Fluctuations of a Single-Domain Particle,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.1677).

title: Identifiability of magnetic Hamiltonians
open: Determine which combinations of scattering, thermodynamics, and local probes uniquely constrain exchange, anisotropy, and multispin interactions, quantifying remaining equivalent models.
status: Spin-wave tools efficiently test specified Hamiltonians. A good spectral fit does not establish uniqueness when momentum coverage is limited or interactions are omitted.
why: Makes proposed mechanisms testable beyond compatibility with selected data.
key_works: Tóth and Lake (2015), “Linear spin wave theory for single-Q incommensurate magnetic structures,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-8984/27/16/166002).

title: Complete vector magnetization tomography
open: Reconstruct all three magnetization components inside buried structures with useful spatial resolution and quantified null spaces, limited-angle artifacts, and uncertainty.
status: Hard-X-ray vector nanotomography demonstrated internal textures in 2017. Absorption, angular access, and inverse-problem ambiguities still constrain unique reconstruction.
why: Reveals internal reversal sites and defects missed by surface imaging.
key_works: Donnelly et al. (2017), “Three-dimensional magnetization structures revealed with X-ray vector nanotomography,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature23006).

title: Nonrepeatable three-dimensional reversal movies
open: Image one nonrepeatable reversal throughout a three-dimensional specimen with enough spatial and temporal resolution to identify nucleation and propagation.
status: Pump–probe magnetic laminography demonstrated 70 ps resolution in 2020. Reconstructing stochastic individual events remains distinct from averaging repeatable cycles.
why: Tests microscopic failure and avalanche mechanisms directly.
key_works: Donnelly et al. (2020), “Time-resolved imaging of three-dimensional nanoscale magnetization dynamics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-020-0649-x).

title: Artifact-resistant magnetometry of weak signals
open: Establish reproducible protocols separating intrinsic weak magnetism from substrates, contamination, remanent instrument fields, and positioning errors at the claimed sensitivity.
status: SQUID studies document these artifacts and mitigation methods. Dilute, interfacial, and small-volume samples still require independent confirmation beyond uncertain background subtraction.
why: Prevents false discoveries and incorrect phase assignments.
key_works: Sawicki, Stefanowicz, and Ney (2011), “Sensitive SQUID magnetometry for studying nanomagnetism,” [arXiv:1101.4764](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.4764).

title: Processing-to-property magnetic materials atlas
subfield: Magnetic data, benchmarks, and scientific infrastructure
open: Link composition and magnetic symmetry to synthesis, microstructure, specimen shape, measurement protocol, and temperature-dependent hysteresis with provenance and uncertainty.
status: MAGNDATA supplies structured magnetic-order information, and databases support computational screening. The proposed joined atlas requires substantially more than structures or isolated moment values.
why: Supports reproducible comparison and discovery of manufacturable magnets.
key_works: Gallego et al. (2016), “MAGNDATA: towards a database of magnetic structures. I. The commensurate case,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1107/S1600576716012863); Horton et al. (2019), “High-throughput prediction of the ground-state collinear magnetic order of inorganic materials using Density Functional Theory,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-019-0199-7).

title: Negative-result database for magnet synthesis
subfield: Magnetic data, benchmarks, and scientific infrastructure
open: Collect failed syntheses, lost coercivity, unstable samples, and unsuccessful replications with enough process detail to distinguish unpromising chemistry from unexplored processing.
status: Learning from failed experiments has been demonstrated in materials discovery. A magnetic resource must additionally capture phase purity, calibration, and failed heat-treatment trajectories.
why: Reduces repeated dead ends and publication-driven training bias.
key_works: Raccuglia et al. (2016), “Machine-learning-assisted materials discovery using failed experiments,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17439); Gallego et al. (2016), “MAGNDATA: towards a database of magnetic structures. I. The commensurate case,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1107/S1600576716012863).

title: Blind cross-laboratory magnetic-loss prediction
subfield: Magnetic data, benchmarks, and scientific infrastructure
open: Benchmark loss models on undisclosed manufacturing lots, laboratories, instruments, transient waveforms, and thermal histories, scoring uncertainty and calibration alongside mean error.
status: MagNet provides open measurements, and MagNetX extends them to transients. Random splits from shared specimens do not establish transfer to independently produced material.
why: Makes learned models dependable for component selection.
key_works: Li et al. (2022), “MagNet: An Open-Source Database for Data-Driven Magnetic Core Loss Modeling,” [publication](https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/magnet-an-open-source-database-for-data-driven-magnetic-core-loss/); Kwon et al. (2025), “MagNetX: Extending the MagNet Database for Modeling Power Magnetics in Transient,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/APEC48143.2025.10977252).

title: Stochastic multiscale micromagnetics benchmark
subfield: Magnetic data, benchmarks, and scientific infrastructure
open: Extend reference problems to thermal switching distributions, atomistic–continuum interfaces, realistic defects, and competing discretizations, with converged reference uncertainty.
status: NIST’s µMAG activity has maintained standard problems since the 1990s. Deterministic agreement does not validate rare thermal events or coupled multiscale dynamics.
why: Detects numerical artifacts before they become proposed mechanisms.
key_works: Donahue and Porter (1999), “OOMMF User’s Guide, Version 1.0,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.6376); NIST, “µMAG: Micromagnetic Modeling Activity Group,” [project](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/mmag-micromagnetic-modeling-activity-group).

title: Shared ground truth for multimodal magnetic microscopy
subfield: Magnetic data, benchmarks, and scientific infrastructure
open: Release co-registered magnetic, chemical, strain, and three-dimensional structural measurements of identical specimens, including raw data and instrument responses.
status: Individual tomography and correlative studies exist. A reusable shared-specimen benchmark for competing reconstructions and inverse-design methods remains an infrastructure target.
why: Separates algorithmic progress from differences in samples and preprocessing.
key_works: Donnelly et al. (2017), “Three-dimensional magnetization structures revealed with X-ray vector nanotomography,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature23006); Bolyachkin et al. (2024), “Tomography-based digital twin of Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01218-5).

title: Nanoscale imaging through realistic sensor stand-off
open: Improve the joint resolution–sensitivity–bandwidth frontier when sensors must remain outside encapsulation, buried layers, or necessary protective coatings.
status: NV magnetometry enables high-resolution ambient sensing. Short-wavelength magnetic fields decay rapidly with distance, so sensitivity alone cannot restore information lost at realistic stand-off.
why: Extends nanoscale magnetometry to operating devices and protected samples.
key_works: Barry et al. (2020), “Sensitivity optimization for NV-diamond magnetometry,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.92.015004).

title: Practical broadband quantum advantage in magnetometry
open: Demonstrate a compact magnetometer using squeezing or entanglement that outperforms the best separable-probe protocol at matched volume, photon flux, bandwidth, and total power, including preparation and readout.
status: Quantum sensing and strong NV sensitivity improvements are established; a 2024 ensemble instrument improved performance. Complete resource-accounted advantage remains a stronger target.
why: Enables smaller field instruments for science, navigation, and inspection.
key_works: Barry et al. (2024), “Sensitive ac and dc magnetometry with nitrogen-vacancy-center ensembles in diamond,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevApplied.22.044069).

title: Wearable magnetometry during unrestricted movement
open: Maintain calibrated multichannel biomagnetic measurements during large rotations and translations in changing ambient fields, with practical shielding, heat, and power budgets.
status: Wearable optically pumped MEG was demonstrated in 2018. Motion artifacts, gradients, heading errors, and crosstalk remain barriers to unrestricted operation.
why: Makes biomagnetic sensing useful beyond stationary controlled experiments.
key_works: Boto et al. (2018), “Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature26147).

title: Low-noise lightweight magnetic shielding
open: Optimize shielding factor, bandwidth, weight, remanence, and thermally generated noise together, including joints, stress, and aging in complete enclosures.
status: Ferrite shields reduce Johnson-current noise relative to conductive shields. Magnetic-loss noise and low-frequency drift still constrain total performance.
why: Improves measurements limited by noise from the shield itself.
key_works: Kornack, Smullin, Lee, and Romalis (2007), “A low-noise ferrite magnetic shield,” [arXiv:physics/0703115](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0703115).

title: Causal identification of the avian magnetic receptor
open: Identify the receptor and cellular pathway necessary and sufficient for magnetic compass behavior, connecting molecular perturbation to controlled behavioral loss and rescue.
status: Investigated for decades. European-robin cryptochrome 4 shows magnetic sensitivity in vitro, but that alone does not establish its causal role in a living bird.
why: Resolves a major sensory mechanism and could inspire chemical sensors.
key_works: Xu et al. (2021), “Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9); Hore and Mouritsen (2016), “The Radical-Pair Mechanism of Magnetoreception,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-biophys-032116-094545).

title: Anatomical identification of a magnetite-based receptor
open: Find a reproducible magnetite-containing sensory structure whose mechanics, innervation, and perturbation establish magnetic transduction rather than ordinary iron storage.
status: Proposed iron-rich pigeon-beak receptors were shown to be macrophages in 2012. This correction does not exclude every magnetite-based mechanism; a causally validated receptor remains missing.
why: Distinguishes competing mechanisms of animal magnetic sensing.
key_works: Treiber et al. (2012), “Clusters of iron-rich cells in the upper beak of pigeons are macrophages not magnetosensitive neurons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11046).

title: Amplification of Earth-field radical-pair signals
open: Show how small field-dependent changes in radical chemistry become robust neural signals under physiological noise, turnover, orientation disorder, and realistic illumination.
status: Radical-pair theory and purified-protein experiments establish plausible sensitivity. The full amplification pathway to directional behavior remains incompletely constrained.
why: Determines whether quantum-chemical sensitivity suffices for biological function.
key_works: Hore and Mouritsen (2016), “The Radical-Pair Mechanism of Magnetoreception,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-biophys-032116-094545); Xu et al. (2021), “Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9).

title: Predictive genetic control of magnetosome crystals
open: Derive a quantitative map from proteins and intracellular chemistry to mineral phase, crystal shape, size distribution, and chain organization, then redesign those outcomes predictably.
status: Essential genes, membrane-biogenesis steps, and heterologous magnetization are established. A programmable nucleation-and-growth mechanism remains beyond identifying necessary genes.
why: Connects biomineralization mechanisms to precision particle fabrication.
key_works: Uebe and Schüler (2016), “Magnetosome biogenesis in magnetotactic bacteria,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrmicro.2016.99); Raschdorf et al. (2016), “Genetic and Ultrastructural Analysis Reveals the Key Players and Initial Steps of Bacterial Magnetosome Membrane Biogenesis,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1006101).

title: Tenfold more productive magnetosome manufacturing
open: Increase purified, specification-compliant output per reactor-hour tenfold against a declared baseline without sacrificing uniformity, magnetic response, contamination control, or production stability.
status: Gene-cluster amplification increased production in 2016. This proposed target concerns complete production and purification, including oxygen control and consistency.
why: Could make biologically manufactured particles economically useful.
key_works: Lohße et al. (2016), “Overproduction of Magnetosomes by Genomic Amplification of Biosynthesis-Related Gene Clusters in a Magnetotactic Bacterium,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.03860-15).

title: Predicting nanoparticle heating inside cells
open: Predict dissipated power from measured particle arrangement, intracellular immobilization, anisotropy, and applied field, including interactions and changing aggregation.
status: Relaxation models explain controlled suspensions. Intracellular clustering and suppressed Brownian rotation alter the conditions, so suspension measurements do not establish in-cell performance.
why: Makes magnetic heating doses physically interpretable.
key_works: Bender et al. (2017), “Structural and magnetic properties of multi-core nanoparticles analysed using a generalised numerical inversion method,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep45990); Wells et al. (2021), “Challenges and recommendations for magnetic hyperthermia characterization measurements,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/02656736.2021.1892837).

title: Validating nanoscale magnetic hot-spot claims
open: Determine which reported local temperature elevations survive independent thermometry and controls for optical artifacts, chemical response, and bulk heating, consistent with measured power.
status: Large steady local-gradient claims face quantitative challenges. Artifact-controlled tests appeared in 2020; disputed biological interpretations still require mechanism-specific confirmation.
why: Distinguishes thermal actuation from alternative magnetic or chemical effects.
key_works: Davis et al. (2020), “Nanoscale Heat Transfer from Magnetic Nanoparticles and Ferritin in an Alternating Magnetic Field,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bpj.2020.01.028).

title: Traceable magnetic-hyperthermia power measurements
open: Establish reference particles and interlaboratory protocols producing agreement between calorimetric and magnetic power measurements, with complete field, mass, and heat-loss uncertainties.
status: The RADIOMAG consortium published recommendations in 2021. Routine comparability across instruments and biologically relevant conditions remains a practical target.
why: Enables defensible comparison of particle designs and heating experiments.
key_works: Wells et al. (2021), “Challenges and recommendations for magnetic hyperthermia characterization measurements,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/02656736.2021.1892837).

title: Quantitative human-scale magnetic particle imaging
open: Recover absolute tracer concentration in human-sized anatomy while meeting defined resolution, frame-rate, heating, stimulation, and calibration requirements across realistic tracer environments.
status: Human-scale construction is established; a 2025 brain-imaging prototype reported approximately 5–7 mm phantom resolution. Quantitative in-vivo transfer remains more demanding.
why: Enables traceable particle tracking and image-guided interventions.
key_works: Gleich and Weizenecker (2005), “Tomographic imaging using the nonlinear response of magnetic particles,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature03808); Mattingly et al. (2025), “Design, construction and validation of a magnetic particle imaging (MPI) system for human brain imaging,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6560/ad9db0).

title: Deep, selective magnetic drug targeting
open: Demonstrate externally controlled delivery to a specified deep target against blood flow, with localization and measured target-to-off-target dose improvement under practical field constraints.
status: Magnetic targeting and shallow demonstrations exist. Deep localization faces decaying gradients, biological transport barriers, and control limitations.
why: Could enable spatially selective delivery using magnetic carriers.
key_works: Shapiro et al. (2015), “Open challenges in magnetic drug targeting,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/wnan.1311).

title: Fluctuating trimerons above the Verwey transition
open: Determine the populations, lifetimes, and interactions of localized electronic units above magnetite’s Verwey transition, explaining transport and structure across doping and temperature.
status: The transition dates to 1939; the low-temperature charge/orbital/trimeron structure was resolved in major detail in 2012. The dynamical high-temperature state remains unresolved.
why: Clarifies coupled electronic, lattice, and magnetic ordering in mixed-valence oxides.
key_works: Senn, Wright, and Attfield (2012), “Charge order and three-site distortions in the Verwey structure of magnetite,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10704); Attfield (2022), “Magnetism and the Trimeron Bond,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.2c00275).

title: Unbiased paleointensity from vortex-state grains
open: Recover ancient field strength from nonuniform magnetic grains using validated models of blocking, unblocking, domain changes, and geological aging.
status: Single-domain theory provides a foundation, but many rocks contain vortex states. A 2022 study showed how unequal blocking and unblocking can invalidate standard protocols.
why: Improves quantitative histories of planetary magnetic fields.
key_works: Nagy et al. (2022), “Chasing Tails: Insights From Micromagnetic Modeling for Thermomagnetic Recording in Non-Uniform Magnetic Structures,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022GL101032).

title: Dating the magnetization of Hadean zircons
open: Establish when individual inclusions acquired remanence independently of host-zircon crystallization age, reconciling conflicting interpretations of the earliest geodynamo record.
status: Studies report Hadean magnetic signals, including supporting analyses in 2020. Later alteration and remagnetization must be tested inclusion by inclusion.
why: Constrains early core evolution and Earth’s surface environment.
key_works: Tarduno et al. (2020), “Paleomagnetism indicates that primary magnetite in zircon records a strong Hadean geodynamo,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916553117); Weiss et al. (2015), “Pervasive remagnetization of detrital zircon host rocks in the Jack Hills, Western Australia and implications for records of the early geodynamo,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epsl.2015.07.067).

title: A spatially resolved lunar magnetic-field history
open: Reconstruct field strength and geometry through time from independently dated samples across both hemispheres, separating dynamo remanence from impacts, anomalies, and alteration.
status: Chang’e samples now supplement Apollo records. Chang’e-6 basalt provides a roughly 2.8-billion-year-old farside constraint; sparse sampling still prevents a unique global history.
why: Tests competing lunar dynamo and interior-evolution models.
key_works: Cai et al. (2025; online 2024), “A reinforced lunar dynamo recorded by Chang’e-6 farside basalt,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08526-2).

title: Recovering geomagnetic events blurred by sediment lock-in
open: Infer remanence-acquisition kernels from independent sediment measurements and recover short excursions without confusing delayed lock-in with field chronology.
status: Modeling has quantified smoothing and missing events since at least 2004. Sedimentation, bioturbation, grain size, and diagenesis prevent universal corrections.
why: Makes magnetic records more reliable clocks for environmental history.
key_works: Roberts and Winklhofer (2004), “Why are geomagnetic excursions not always recorded in sediments? Constraints from post-depositional remanent magnetization lock-in modelling,” [publication](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012821X04005242).

title: Unambiguous identification of ancient magnetofossils
open: Distinguish biogenic magnetite or greigite from abiotic look-alikes after dissolution, recrystallization, chain collapse, and aging using independently testable multimodal criteria.
status: Morphology, microscopy, and FORC central ridges provide evidence. No single magnetic signature proves biological origin under every preservation history.
why: Enables defensible reconstruction of ancient microbial ecosystems.
key_works: Heslop et al. (2014), “Characterizing magnetofossils from first-order reversal curve (FORC) central ridge signatures,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/2014GC005291); Roberts et al. (2011), “Magnetic properties of sedimentary greigite (Fe3S4): An update,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1029/2010RG000336).

title: Direct recycling of heterogeneous magnet scrap
subfield: Circular manufacturing, supply chains, and funding
open: Recycle mixed Nd–Fe–B feedstocks into specification-compliant magnets despite realistic variations in coatings, oxygen, Dy/Tb content, adhesives, and alloy composition.
status: Hydrogen processing and magnet-to-magnet recycling are established. Controlled-feedstock demonstrations do not determine impurity tolerance and yield for heterogeneous post-consumer streams.
why: Preserves material value and reduces primary rare-earth demand.
key_works: Walton et al. (2015), “The use of hydrogen to separate and recycle neodymium–iron–boron-type magnets from electronic waste,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2015.05.033); Yang et al. (2017), “REE Recovery from End-of-Life NdFeB Permanent Magnet Scrap: A Critical Review,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40831-016-0090-4).

title: Economical recovery of embedded magnets
subfield: Circular manufacturing, supply chains, and funding
open: Automate identification, necessary demagnetization, and removal from diverse motors and electronics without destroying reusable material or exceeding recoverable value.
status: Hydrogen-assisted separation and product-specific disassembly work. Adhesives, inaccessible geometry, coatings, and unknown histories complicate general high-throughput recovery.
why: Converts dispersed end-of-life magnets into accessible feedstock.
key_works: Walton et al. (2015), “The use of hydrogen to separate and recycle neodymium–iron–boron-type magnets from electronic waste,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2015.05.033); Yang et al. (2017), “REE Recovery from End-of-Life NdFeB Permanent Magnet Scrap: A Critical Review,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40831-016-0090-4).

title: Low-waste separation of magnet rare earths
subfield: Circular manufacturing, supply chains, and funding
open: Recover and separate Nd, Pr, Dy, and Tb from realistic waste with demonstrated reagent recycling, impurity rejection, complete waste accounting, and competitive scaled cost.
status: Hydrometallurgical, pyrometallurgical, and electrochemical routes exist. High recovery from clean laboratory solutions does not establish a favorable complete process.
why: Reduces environmental and supply burdens when direct recycling is unsuitable.
key_works: Binnemans et al. (2013), “Recycling of rare earths: a critical review,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2012.12.037); IEA (2025), “Innovation in mining, refining and recycling to promote diversification,” [report chapter](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2025/innovation-in-mining-refining-and-recycling-to-promote-diversification).

title: Lifecycle comparisons with equal magnetic service
subfield: Circular manufacturing, supply chains, and funding
open: Compare virgin, directly recycled, chemically recycled, and substitute magnets per unit of delivered service over their lifetimes, including redesign, failure, and recycling allocation.
status: Lifecycle assessments exist, but results depend on system boundaries, electricity, yield, and functional units. Equal mass need not mean equal service.
why: Identifies substitutions and recycling routes that reduce total impacts.
key_works: Jin et al. (2016), “Comparative Life Cycle Assessment of NdFeB Magnets: Virgin Production versus Magnet-to-Magnet Recycling,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procir.2016.03.013).

title: Financing qualified magnet production through price cycles
subfield: Circular manufacturing, supply chains, and funding
open: Design and evaluate procurement, offtake, or risk-sharing arrangements sustaining qualified production through volatile prices without permanently insulating poor performance.
status: The IEA’s 2026 assessment identifies midstream and magnet-manufacturing gaps. Which arrangements produce durable diversification at acceptable public cost remains an implementation and evaluation question.
why: Converts demonstrated materials into viable manufacturing capacity.
key_works: IEA (2026), “Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026,” [report](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2026).

title: Shared pilot lines for independent magnet qualification
subfield: Circular manufacturing, supply chains, and funding
open: Establish sustainable access to pilot-scale powder production, alignment, consolidation, coating, and qualification so independent teams can measure yield and service performance beyond laboratory batches.
status: Research facilities and company pilots exist. Affordable repeatable access connecting all relevant processing and qualification stages remains the proposed gap.
why: Addresses the transition from publication to qualified industrial components.
key_works: Gutfleisch et al. (2011), “Magnetic Materials and Devices for the 21st Century: Stronger, Lighter, and More Energy Efficient,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.201002180); IEA (2026), “Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026,” [report](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2026).

title: Traceable inventories of magnets in use and waste
subfield: Circular manufacturing, supply chains, and funding
open: Build auditable product-to-alloy inventories predicting when and where magnets become recoverable, with uncertainty in composition, lifetime, collection, reuse, and exports.
status: Critical-mineral outlooks and aggregate material-flow studies provide estimates. Recycling decisions require finer product-level composition and availability than aggregate tonnage supplies.
why: Connects recycling and collection capacity to actual future feedstocks.
key_works: IEA (2025), “Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025,” [report](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2025); Binnemans et al. (2013), “Recycling of rare earths: a critical review,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2012.12.037).

title: Haldane gap for the spin-1 Heisenberg chain
open: Prove a strictly positive thermodynamic spectral gap for the translation-invariant, nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic spin-1 Heisenberg chain with periodic boundaries, with a lower bound independent of chain length.
status: Proposed in 1983; extensive numerical and experimental support exists. The rigorous gap of the AKLT chain does not prove the Heisenberg result because the Hamiltonians differ.
why: Establishes the foundational distinction between integer-spin and half-integer-spin quantum magnets.
key_works: Haldane (1983), “Nonlinear Field Theory of Large-Spin Heisenberg Antiferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.50.1153); Affleck et al. (1987), “Rigorous Results on Valence-Bond Ground States in Antiferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.799).

title: Rigorous Néel order in the square-lattice spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet
open: Prove nonzero staggered magnetization in the infinite-volume ground state of the nearest-neighbor square-lattice spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet.
status: Decades of numerical evidence support ordering. Reflection-positivity arguments establish related higher-spin and higher-dimensional cases but leave this central case open.
why: Puts a standard microscopic model of antiferromagnetism on rigorous footing.
key_works: Dyson, Lieb, and Simon (1978), “Phase transitions in quantum spin systems with isotropic and nonisotropic interactions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01106729); Tasaki (2020), *Physics and Mathematics of Quantum Many-Body Systems*, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-41265-4).

title: Low-spin honeycomb XY order
open: Prove ground-state long-range order for the nearest-neighbor honeycomb XY magnet at spin 1/2, and extend the proof through the other unresolved low-spin cases.
status: Wojtkiewicz, Wohlfeld, and Oleś proved honeycomb ordering for spin at least 2 in 2023. The rigorous bound does not reach the low-spin cases supported by spin-wave calculations.
why: Tests how low coordination and quantum fluctuations constrain ordering proofs.
key_works: Wojtkiewicz, Wohlfeld, and Oleś (2023), “Long-range order in the XY model on the honeycomb lattice,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.107.064409).

title: Positive-temperature quantum Heisenberg ferromagnetism
open: Prove spontaneous magnetization at sufficiently low positive temperature for the nearest-neighbor quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet on the three-dimensional cubic lattice, particularly for spin 1/2.
status: A longstanding mathematical-physics problem. Rigorous low-temperature free-energy asymptotics agree with spin-wave theory, but do not establish spontaneous magnetization.
why: Supplies a missing rigorous explanation of the simplest quantum ferromagnet.
key_works: Lieb (1999), “Long Range Order for the Quantum Heisenberg Model,” [problem statement](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~aizenman/OpenProblems_MathPhys/9901.HeisenbergFerr.html); Correggi, Giuliani, and Seiringer (2015), “Validity of the spin-wave approximation for the free energy of the Heisenberg ferromagnet,” [arXiv:1312.7873](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7873).

title: Mass generation in the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg magnet
open: Prove exponential decay of correlations at every positive temperature in the nearest-neighbor two-dimensional O(3) model, and establish the low-temperature correlation-length asymptotics.
status: The field-theory prediction dates to 1975. Aru, Garban, and Sepúlveda’s 2025 work resolves parts of competing geometric arguments without proving the full lattice mass-gap statement.
why: Connects an elementary magnet to nonperturbative mass generation.
key_works: Aru, Garban, and Sepúlveda (2025), “Percolation for 2D Classical Heisenberg Model and Exit Sets of Vector Valued GFF,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-024-05208-y).

title: Nearest-neighbor kagome Heisenberg ground state
open: Determine the thermodynamic gap, topological order, and broken symmetries of the spin-1/2 nearest-neighbor kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet, with mutually consistent numerical extrapolations.
status: Gapped and gapless liquid descriptions remain competitive. A 2026 comment challenges the sampling underlying a 2025 spinon pair-density-wave claim; unusually low variational energies alone do not settle the state.
why: Resolves a central benchmark for two-dimensional fractionalization.
key_works: Yan, Huse, and White (2011), “Spin-Liquid Ground State of the S = 1/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1201080); Kamal et al. (2026), “Comment on ‘Spin-1/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet: Machine Learning Discovery of the Spinon Pair-Density-Wave Ground State’,” [arXiv:2605.28861](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28861).

title: Square-lattice J1–J2 intermediate phase
open: Establish whether the spin-1/2 square-lattice J1–J2 antiferromagnet contains a finite spin-liquid region between Néel and valence-bond order, and determine its boundaries and gap.
status: Studied since the 1980s. Numerical methods disagree over a narrow liquid region, plaquette versus columnar order, and finite-size extrapolation; DMRG supports plaquette order in part of the nonmagnetic regime.
why: Distinguishes a stable liquid from a broad transition crossover.
key_works: Gong et al. (2014), “Plaquette Ordered Phase and Quantum Phase Diagram in the Spin-1/2 J1–J2 Square Heisenberg Model,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.027201).

title: Triangular J1–J2 spin-liquid universality
open: Determine whether the intermediate phase of the triangular spin-1/2 J1–J2 model is a stable Dirac liquid, a gapped liquid, or another phase, and identify its universal observables.
status: DMRG established a strong candidate in 2015. Recent dynamical calculations support Dirac descriptions, but finite-cylinder and approximation dependence remain unresolved.
why: Provides quantitative predictions for triangular magnetic materials.
key_works: Zhu and White (2015), “Spin liquid phase of the S=1/2 J1–J2 Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice,” [arXiv:1502.04831](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04831); Willsher and Knolle (2025; revised 2026), “Dynamics and stability of U(1) spin liquids beyond mean-field theory: Triangular-lattice J1–J2 Heisenberg model,” [arXiv:2503.13831](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13831).

title: Spin-1/2 pyrochlore Heisenberg ground-state selection
open: Identify the infinite-system ground state and excitation spectrum of the nearest-neighbor spin-1/2 pyrochlore Heisenberg antiferromagnet, resolving competing valence-bond crystals and liquids.
status: Unsettled after roughly three decades. A 2025 unrestricted variational study finds nearly degenerate, structurally distinct crystals selected by tiny further-neighbor exchanges.
why: Establishes what three-dimensional geometric frustration alone produces.
key_works: Cheng and Li (2025), “Closely competing valence bond crystal orders in the ground state of the spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model on the pyrochlore lattice…” [arXiv:2509.13746](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13746), title abbreviated.

title: Hyperkagome Heisenberg ground state
open: Determine whether the spin-1/2 nearest-neighbor hyperkagome antiferromagnet has a gapless liquid, gapped topological liquid, or valence-bond order, including its low-temperature thermodynamics.
status: Candidate states have been investigated since hyperkagome materials were identified. A 2024 thermodynamic analysis still requires alternative low-energy assumptions and obtains scenario-dependent estimates.
why: Separates intrinsic three-dimensional liquid physics from material disorder.
key_works: Hutak et al. (2024), “Thermodynamics of the S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.110.054428).

title: Honeycomb Néel-to-plaquette transition
open: Resolve whether the spin-1/2 honeycomb J1–J2 model loses Néel order through a continuous deconfined transition, a weak first-order transition, or an intervening phase.
status: Numerical and coupled-cluster studies since 2011 identify nearby plaquette order. Small order parameters and long crossover scales obstruct an asymptotic diagnosis.
why: Tests how lattice symmetry and monopoles affect unconventional criticality.
key_works: Farnell et al. (2011), “Frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice: A candidate for deconfined quantum criticality,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.84.012403).

title: Antiferromagnetic Kitaev model in a [111] field
open: Identify the thermodynamic phases between the low-field Kitaev liquid and the polarized state, including whether the intermediate regime is gapless, topological, or symmetry-breaking.
status: The zero-field spin-1/2 model is solved; the finite-field problem remains contested. Competing U(1), gapped, and chiral descriptions persist, with additional intermediate-field order reported computationally in 2025.
why: Supplies the reference phase diagram for high-field Kitaev materials.
key_works: Hickey and Trebst (2019), “Emergence of a field-driven U(1) spin liquid in the Kitaev honeycomb model,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-08459-9); Liu et al. (2025), “Emergence of quantum spin liquid and spin-flop phase in Kitaev antiferromagnets in a [111] magnetic field,” [arXiv:2509.04141](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04141).

title: Topological identity of the spin-1 Kitaev liquid
open: Establish the gap, emergent gauge structure, and quasiparticle statistics of the isotropic spin-1 honeycomb Kitaev model using controlled thermodynamic diagnostics.
status: The higher-spin model lacks the spin-1/2 model’s exact solution. Tensor networks identify liquid regimes and competing nematic phases without fully determining topological content.
why: Extends fractionalization beyond effective spin-1/2 compounds.
key_works: Mashiko and Okubo (2024), “Quantum phase transition between spin liquid and spin nematics in spin-1 Kitaev honeycomb model,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.033110).

title: Intrinsic low-energy gap of herbertsmithite
open: Determine the defect-free kagome contribution to the zero-field gap and low-energy spectrum of ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2, separating interlayer Cu defects and local disorder.
status: Gapped NMR evidence appeared in 2015, while other probes support gapless behavior. A 2026 study probes spinon-mediated defect dynamics and discusses the continuing disagreement.
why: Turns broad excitation continua into a discriminating ground-state diagnosis.
key_works: Fu et al. (2015), “Evidence for a gapped spin-liquid ground state in a kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aab2120); Takahashi et al. (2026), “Spinon mediation of witness spin dynamics in herbertsmithite,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03303-6).

title: Topological certification of Zn-barlowite
open: Establish whether Cu3Zn(OH)6FBr realizes a bulk topological spin liquid, and determine how site mixing changes its gap and quasiparticles.
status: A 2017 NMR study reported a gap with field dependence consistent with spin-1/2 spinons. This does not uniquely establish topological order or eliminate defect uncertainty.
why: Could establish a chemically distinct kagome liquid platform.
key_works: Feng et al. (2017), “Gapped Spin-1/2 Spinon Excitations in a New Kagome Quantum Spin Liquid Compound Cu3Zn(OH)6FBr,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/0256-307X/34/7/077502).

title: Topology of the kagome one-ninth magnetization plateau
open: Identify the order, topological content, and excitations of the one-ninth plateau in YCu3(OD)6+xBr3−x, and connect them to the ideal kagome Hamiltonian.
status: The plateau has been observed. Thermodynamic and Raman measurements reported in 2023 support entangled excitations, but several microscopic plateau states remain possible.
why: Tests fractionalized incompressible phases in an accessible field window.
key_works: Jeon et al. (2023), “One-ninth magnetization plateau stabilized by spin entanglement in a kagome antiferromagnet,” [arXiv:2311.11619](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11619).

title: Intrinsic versus disorder-generated liquid behavior in YbMgGaO4
open: Determine which low-energy signatures survive removal of Mg/Ga-induced exchange randomness, and whether the idealized material Hamiltonian supports a liquid.
status: Liquid claims date to 2015. Random-exchange calculations in 2017 reproduced important continuum features, showing that a broad continuum and absent order are insufficient discriminants.
why: Distinguishes intrinsic fractionalization from disorder-generated states.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2017), “Disorder-Induced Mimicry of a Spin Liquid in YbMgGaO4,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.157201).

title: NaYbSe2 ground-state excitation structure
open: Decide whether NaYbSe2 has a spinon Fermi surface, a small intrinsic gap, or a disorder-influenced state, using one Hamiltonian consistent with spectroscopy and thermodynamics.
status: A 2021 neutron study proposed a spinon Fermi surface. Subsequent gap and heat-transport studies have not made a continuum uniquely diagnostic of that state.
why: Tests a comparatively clean triangular candidate for fermionic fractionalization.
key_works: Dai et al. (2021), “Spinon Fermi Surface Spin Liquid in a Triangular Lattice Antiferromagnet NaYbSe2,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.11.021044).

title: Mobile versus localized excitations in the dmit organic spin-liquid candidate
open: Reconcile sample-dependent residual thermal conductivity in EtMe3Sb[Pd(dmit)2]2 and determine whether low-energy entropy resides in mobile spinons or localized excitations.
status: Substantial residual transport was reported in 2010; independent 2019 measurements found essentially none. Cooling-rate and sample-quality dependence lack a shared microscopic explanation.
why: Distinguishes a neutral conducting liquid from a disorder-dominated insulator.
key_works: Bourgeois-Hope et al. (2019), “Thermal conductivity of the quantum spin liquid candidate EtMe3Sb[Pd(dmit)2]2: No evidence of mobile gapless excitations,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.9.041051).

title: Hydrogen-disorder versus intrinsic Kitaev physics in H3LiIr2O6
open: Determine whether H3LiIr2O6 is continuously connected to a clean Kitaev liquid or requires hydrogen-position disorder, and predict isotope dependence from the same microscopic model.
status: The candidate emerged in 2018. Deuterated-material studies in 2025 report strong isotope effects, requiring coupled nuclear, lattice, and magnetic dynamics in its interpretation.
why: Establishes whether chemical tuning preserves an intrinsic liquid or creates a random state.
key_works: Kitagawa et al. (2018), “A spin–orbital-entangled quantum liquid on a honeycomb lattice,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature25482); Takayama et al. (2025), “Robust quantum spin liquid state in the presence of giant magnetic isotope effect in D3LiIr2O6,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41535-025-00727-w).

title: Ground-state identity of field-disordered α-RuCl3
open: Determine whether field-disordered α-RuCl3 contains an equilibrium topological liquid, and delimit it against polarized states, residual order, and crossovers.
status: Suppression of zigzag order and excitation continua are established. Field orientation, stacking, and competing Hamiltonians still yield different interpretations.
why: Determines whether the most studied Kitaev candidate reaches the targeted phase.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2017), “Neutron scattering in the proximate quantum spin liquid α-RuCl3,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aah6015); Lefrançois et al. (2022), “Evidence of a Phonon Hall Effect in the Kitaev Spin Liquid Candidate α-RuCl3,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.12.021025).

title: Reproducible half-quantized thermal Hall effect in α-RuCl3
open: Establish a reproducible plateau at the predicted absolute half-quantized thermal Hall value, isolate edge and bulk contributions, and explain sample and geometry dependence.
status: Half quantization was reported in 2018; other experiments emphasize phonons or unquantized signals. A 2025 constriction experiment supports chiral fermionic edge transport without settling every quantization question.
why: Tests a leading proposed signature of non-Abelian magnetic excitations.
key_works: Kasahara et al. (2018), “Majorana quantization and half-integer thermal quantum Hall effect in a Kitaev spin liquid,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0274-0); Zhang et al. (2025), “Evidence of chiral fermion edge modes through geometric engineering of thermal Hall in α-RuCl3,” [arXiv:2505.05417](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05417).

title: Independent Hamiltonian identification for Na2Co2TeO6
open: Constrain the exchange Hamiltonian sufficiently to distinguish competing Kitaev-dominated and other descriptions, then test its predicted high-field fractionalization.
status: A 2025 model with dominant antiferromagnetic Kitaev exchange reproduces thermodynamics and predicts an intermediate liquid. Selected successful fits do not establish uniqueness.
why: Determines whether cobaltates provide a reliable route to antiferromagnetic Kitaev physics.
key_works: Li et al. (2025), “Kitaev-derived Gapless Spin Liquid in the K–J–Γ–Γ′ Quantum Magnet Na2Co2TeO6,” [arXiv:2509.08821](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08821).

title: Flux-sector identification in Ce2Zr2O7
subfield: Spin ice and three-dimensional emergent electrodynamics
open: Determine the emergent flux sector and dipolar versus octupolar gauge structure through a consistent quantitative account of photon, spinon, and field-dependent spectra.
status: Photon-like and fractionalized excitations were reported in 2024. The remaining target is overdetermined verification of the full low-energy gauge theory.
why: Converts emergent-electrodynamics evidence into predictive material theory.
key_works: Gao et al. (2024), “Emergent photons and fractionalized excitations in a quantum spin liquid,” [arXiv:2404.04207](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04207).

title: Dynamical gauge theory of Ce2Sn2O7
subfield: Spin ice and three-dimensional emergent electrodynamics
open: Establish the low-energy gauge excitations and flux sector, distinguishing a coherent octupolar U(1) liquid from disorder-modified alternatives.
status: Neutron measurements in 2020 identified octupolar correlations and a continuum consistent with spinons. A complete photon dispersion and unique gauge-sector assignment remain missing.
why: Tests whether magnetic multipoles generate a distinct family of quantum liquids.
key_works: Sibille et al. (2020), “A quantum liquid of magnetic octupoles on the pyrochlore lattice,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-020-0827-7).

title: Random transverse fields in Pr2Zr2O7
subfield: Spin ice and three-dimensional emergent electrodynamics
open: Determine whether random strain and transverse fields permit a coherent U(1) liquid at the lowest energies or instead produce a glass or quadrupolar state.
status: Two 2017 studies established the importance of random strain and proposed different disorder-mediated pictures. A common quantitative defect-to-phase theory remains incomplete.
why: Reveals whether disorder can assist emergent electrodynamics.
key_works: Wen et al. (2017), “Disordered Route to the Coulomb Quantum Spin Liquid: Random Transverse Fields on Spin Ice in Pr2Zr2O7,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.107206); Martin et al. (2017), “Disorder and Quantum spin ice,” [arXiv:1708.01845](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01845).

title: Stoichiometry-selected low-temperature phases of Tb2Ti2O7
subfield: Spin ice and three-dimensional emergent electrodynamics
open: Explain quantitatively how tiny off-stoichiometry, magnetoelastic coupling, and quadrupolar interactions select ordered or liquid-like low-temperature states.
status: Quadrupolar order has been identified in suitable compositions. Strong sample dependence and coupled crystal-field/lattice modes still obstruct a unified microscopic phase diagram.
why: Explains why nominally identical frustrated magnets have different ground states.
key_works: Takatsu et al. (2016), “Quadrupole Order in the Frustrated Pyrochlore Tb2+xTi2−xO7+y,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.217201).

title: Zero-field continuum in Yb2Ti2O7
subfield: Spin ice and three-dimensional emergent electrodynamics
open: Derive the broad low-field continuum from a Hamiltonian independently constrained at high field, including competition between phases and sample defects.
status: High-field quasiparticles and exchanges are established; their breakdown at lower field was measured in 2017. The resulting continuum lacks a fully predictive account.
why: Distinguishes strongly interacting magnons from fractionalization.
key_works: Thompson et al. (2017), “Quasiparticle Breakdown and Spin Hamiltonian of the Frustrated Quantum Pyrochlore Yb2Ti2O7 in a Magnetic Field,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.057203).

title: Equilibrium ordering of Dy2Ti2O7
subfield: Spin ice and three-dimensional emergent electrodynamics
open: Reach and identify the true equilibrium low-temperature state, distinguishing competing predicted orders from kinetically arrested spin ice.
status: Dipolar models predict eventual ordering, but extraordinarily slow dynamics prevent equilibration. Further-neighbor exchanges produce nearly competing orders and consequential parameter uncertainty.
why: Separates thermodynamic residual entropy from frozen-in entropy.
key_works: Henelius et al. (2016), “Refrustration and competing orders in the prototypical Dy2Ti2O7 spin ice material,” [arXiv:1512.05361](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.05361).

title: Accessible SO(5) deconfined criticality
open: Construct and verify a local two-dimensional magnetic Hamiltonian reaching a genuine SO(5)-symmetric critical fixed point, and establish its relevant operators and basin of attraction.
status: Deconfined criticality was proposed in 2004. Large-scale 2024 J–Q simulations find weak first-order transitions near a proposed multicritical point, leaving access to the point itself unresolved.
why: Determines which unconventional critical behavior survives asymptotically.
key_works: Senthil et al. (2004), “Deconfined Quantum Critical Points,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1091806); Takahashi et al. (2024), “SO(5) multicriticality in two-dimensional quantum magnets,” [arXiv:2405.06607](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06607).

title: Tuning SrCu2(BO3)2 to genuine deconfinement
open: Determine whether field, strain, or composition tuning can reach a continuous plaquette-to-antiferromagnet transition, with scaling distinguishable from weak first-order behavior.
status: Competing pressure-induced phases are established. A 2025 heat-capacity study identifies the zero-field transition as first order; the target is an alternative tuning trajectory.
why: Could provide a bulk-material deconfined critical point.
key_works: Guo et al. (2025), “Deconfined quantum critical point lost in pressurized SrCu2(BO3)2,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42005-025-01976-8).

title: Physical-flavor stability of the Dirac spin liquid
open: Determine the relevance of every symmetry-allowed monopole and interaction at the physical flavor number of QED3 describing triangular and kagome Dirac liquids.
status: Large-flavor arguments establish stable regimes, and lattice symmetries constrain monopoles. Nonperturbative scaling dimensions at physical flavor number remain decisive.
why: Turns parton constructions into reliable predictions of stable phases.
key_works: Hermele et al. (2004), “On the stability of U(1) spin liquids in two dimensions,” [arXiv:cond-mat/0404751](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0404751); Song et al. (2019), “Unifying description of competing orders in two-dimensional quantum magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-11727-3).

title: Controlled theory of a two-dimensional spinon Fermi surface
open: Obtain a controlled physical-flavor theory of a spinon Fermi surface coupled to a dynamical U(1) gauge field, determining stability, exponents, and pairing instabilities.
status: Large-flavor and dimensional expansions provide candidate theories. Singular corrections, pairing, and confinement prevent a generally controlled description of spin-1/2 materials.
why: Predicts thermodynamics and transport in candidate neutral metals.
key_works: Lee (2009), “Low-energy effective theory of Fermi surface coupled with U(1) gauge field in 2+1 dimensions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.80.165102); Mross et al. (2010), “Controlled expansion for certain non-Fermi-liquid metals,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.82.045121).

title: Microscopic origin of Fermi-surface reconstruction in YbRh2Si2
open: Establish whether the field-tuned Fermi-surface change results from Kondo destruction, and connect Hall, spectroscopic, thermodynamic, and magnetic responses through one quantitative theory.
status: Hall-crossover evidence dates to 2004. Finite-temperature extrapolation, multiband transport, and competing low-temperature orders complicate unique interpretation.
why: Tests whether local moments leave the Fermi surface at criticality.
key_works: Paschen et al. (2004), “Hall-effect evolution across a heavy-fermion quantum critical point,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature03129); Kirchner et al. (2020), “Colloquium: Heavy-electron quantum criticality and single-particle spectroscopy,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.92.011002).

title: Universal anomalous scaling in CeCu6−xAux
open: Derive the momentum-dependent magnetic response and anomalous energy/temperature scaling near critical Au concentration from a microscopic theory incorporating disorder and dimensional crossover.
status: Landmark measurements in 2000 established anomalous scaling. Local-criticality models explain important features without uniquely deriving all microscopic ingredients and exponents.
why: Explains a central counterexample to conventional metallic criticality.
key_works: Schröder et al. (2000), “Onset of antiferromagnetism in heavy-fermion metals,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/35030039); Si et al. (2001), “Locally critical quantum phase transitions in strongly correlated metals,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/35101507).

title: Continuous ferromagnetic quantum criticality in clean metals
open: Identify microscopic conditions permitting continuous ferromagnetic criticality despite generic first-order or modulated-order instabilities, and test them quantitatively in CeRh6Ge4 and related exceptions.
status: Soft electronic modes explain widespread avoidance of criticality. Reported pressure-tuned criticality in CeRh6Ge4 leaves the roles of local moments, anisotropy, and dimensionality unresolved.
why: Establishes when ferromagnetic critical fluctuations are accessible.
key_works: Belitz, Kirkpatrick, and Vojta (1999), “First Order Transitions and Multicritical Points in Weak Itinerant Ferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.82.4707); Shen et al. (2020), “Strange-metal behaviour in a pure ferromagnetic Kondo lattice,” [arXiv:1907.10470](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10470).

title: Observable scaling window of the two-dimensional antiferromagnetic metal
open: Determine when asymptotic spin-fermion criticality governs measurable responses before superconductivity, disorder, or other instabilities intervene.
status: A 2017 treatment derived critical exponents in a controlled low-energy regime. Connecting that regime to finite-energy simulations and actual metals remains incomplete.
why: Makes magnetic critical theories falsifiable beyond exponent fitting.
key_works: Schlief, Lunts, and Lee (2017), “Exact Critical Exponents for the Antiferromagnetic Quantum Critical Metal in Two Dimensions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.7.021010).

title: Pure-state organization of the three-dimensional Edwards–Anderson glass
open: Determine the thermodynamic pure-state and overlap structure of the short-range three-dimensional Ising spin glass, distinguishing droplet, replica-symmetry-breaking, and intermediate scenarios.
status: Competing pictures date to the 1980s. Modern simulations find nontrivial overlaps, while 2025 work argues that some apparent replica-symmetry-breaking signatures can arise from finite-size droplets.
why: Determines which mean-field glass features survive in physical magnets.
key_works: Fisher and Huse (1986), “Ordered Phase of Short-Range Ising Spin-Glasses,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.1601); Vedula, Moore, and Sharma (2025), “Nature of spin glass order in physical dimensions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.111.034102).

title: de Almeida–Thouless transition in three dimensions
open: Establish or exclude an equilibrium spin-glass transition at nonzero uniform field in the three-dimensional short-range Edwards–Anderson model.
status: The mean-field instability line dates to 1978. Long crossovers and equilibration problems obstruct the physical-dimensional question; higher-dimensional evidence does not settle it.
why: Decides whether a field destroys or modifies the equilibrium glass phase.
key_works: de Almeida and Thouless (1978), “Stability of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick solution of a spin glass model,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/11/5/028); Young and Katzgraber (2004), “Absence of an Almeida-Thouless Line in Three-Dimensional Spin Glasses,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.207203).

title: Lower critical dimension of spin-glass order in a field
open: Determine the lower critical dimension for the AT transition and the fixed-point structure near that threshold.
status: Perturbation theory near six dimensions has long been problematic. A 2025 study reports a finite-field transition in five dimensions without fixing the lower threshold.
why: Connects conflicting finite-dimensional results through one phase diagram.
key_works: Aguilar-Janita et al. (2025), “Evidence of de Almeida–Thouless line below six dimensions,” [arXiv:2510.14446](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14446).

title: Spin–chirality decoupling in Heisenberg spin glasses
open: Decide whether the isotropic three-dimensional Heisenberg glass has distinct chiral and spin freezing transitions, and determine how weak anisotropy couples them in alloys.
status: Large simulations support separate transitions, while competing analyses emphasize finite-size corrections. The isotropic limit and experimental anisotropy crossover remain unsettled.
why: Identifies the actual frozen degree of freedom in vector-spin glasses.
key_works: Viet and Kawamura (2009), “Numerical Evidence of Spin-Chirality Decoupling in the Three-Dimensional Heisenberg Spin Glass Model,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.027202); Ogawa, Uematsu, and Kawamura (2020), “Monte Carlo studies of the spin-chirality decoupling in the three-dimensional Heisenberg spin glass,” [arXiv:1912.02502](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02502).

title: Operational effective temperature in aging spin glasses
open: Determine when fluctuation–dissipation ratios define a probe-independent effective temperature, and test the proposed connection to equilibrium overlap distributions.
status: Mean-field relations and experiments provide partial support. Probe, frequency, observable, and preparation dependence still limit a universal thermodynamic interpretation.
why: Tests whether nonequilibrium systems admit useful thermodynamic state variables.
key_works: Dahlberg et al. (2025), “Spin-glass dynamics: experiment, theory and simulation,” [arXiv:2412.08381](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08381).

title: Quantitative temperature-chaos account of rejuvenation and memory
open: Predict rejuvenation and memory across arbitrary temperature cycles from independently measured coherence and chaos lengths in a real spin glass.
status: Temperature chaos and numerical rejuvenation are demonstrated. A unified account separating chaos, cumulative aging, finite-time effects, and anisotropy remains open.
why: Turns classic magnetic history dependence into predictive dynamics.
key_works: Dahlberg et al. (2025), “Spin-glass dynamics: experiment, theory and simulation,” [arXiv:2412.08381](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08381).

title: Parity-resolved critical gaps of the three-dimensional quantum spin glass
open: Determine symmetry-resolved gap distributions at the transverse-field transition of a three-dimensional Edwards–Anderson magnet, identifying which gaps control response and annealing.
status: Studied numerically in 1994. Large-scale two-dimensional work in 2024 demonstrates the need to separate gap sectors; the comparable three-dimensional account remains demanding.
why: Relates magnetic criticality to achievable quantum-annealing times.
key_works: Guo, Bhatt, and Huse (1994), “Quantum Critical Behavior of a Three-Dimensional Ising Spin Glass in a Transverse Magnetic Field,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.72.4137); Bernaschi et al. (2024), “The quantum transition of the two-dimensional Ising spin glass,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07647-y).

title: Universality of two-dimensional random-singlet phases
open: Determine whether frustrated and unfrustrated two-dimensional random-singlet magnets share one infrared fixed point, including finite-exponent versus activated scaling and anisotropy stability.
status: Several models possess numerical random-singlet phases. Energy-length and correlation scaling remain model-dependent; 2024–2025 work improves low-energy diagnostics.
why: Provides quantitatively testable alternatives to clean spin liquids.
key_works: Liu et al. (2018), “Random-Singlet Phase in Disordered Two-Dimensional Quantum Magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.8.041040); Peng and Zhang (2024), “Dynamical scaling behavior of the two-dimensional random singlet state in the random Q model,” [arXiv:2408.04533](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04533).

title: Microscopic derivation of isotropic-chain superdiffusion
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Derive the long-time two-point spin-correlation scaling function and temperature-dependent amplitude directly from the quantum Heisenberg chain, controlling hydrodynamic and finite-time corrections.
status: Numerical, quasiparticle, and soliton descriptions support dynamical exponent 3/2. A 2023 fluctuating-hydrodynamic theory captures central features without completing the microscopic derivation.
why: Explains how deterministic quantum dynamics generates anomalous hydrodynamics.
key_works: De Nardis, Gopalakrishnan, and Vasseur (2023), “Nonlinear Fluctuating Hydrodynamics for Kardar-Parisi-Zhang Scaling in Isotropic Spin Chains,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.131.197102).

title: Superdiffusion-to-diffusion crossover under integrability breaking
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Determine the asymptotic transport law and crossover time of weakly nonintegrable SU(2)-symmetric spin chains as functions of perturbation strength and structure.
status: Some perturbations permit long-lived superdiffusion. A 2021 kinetic analysis identifies parametrically long crossovers, leaving accessible simulations unable to distinguish persistent anomalies from eventual diffusion.
why: Establishes whether ideal-chain predictions survive realistic interactions.
key_works: De Nardis, Gopalakrishnan, and Vasseur (2021), “Stability of Superdiffusion in Nearly Integrable Spin Chains,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.057201).

title: Hydrodynamic crossover map in KCuF3
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Measure and predict how transport crosses between one-dimensional superdiffusion, finite-field behavior, and three-dimensional or phonon-dominated regimes.
status: Neutron scattering in 2021 reported KPZ-type two-point scaling. Resolution, anisotropy, and interchain ordering constrain the longest-time regime.
why: Determines the useful experimental window for anomalous quantum transport.
key_works: Scheie et al. (2021), “Detection of Kardar–Parisi–Zhang hydrodynamics in a quantum Heisenberg spin-1/2 chain,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-021-01191-6).

title: Full counting statistics of Heisenberg-chain spin transfer
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Identify the universal transferred-magnetization distribution in the isotropic quantum Heisenberg chain, including higher cumulants and initial-condition dependence.
status: A 2024 experiment on 46 superconducting qubits found superdiffusive first and second moments but disagreement with the original KPZ conjecture in higher moments.
why: Distinguishes theories sharing the same mean transport exponent.
key_works: Rosenberg et al. (2024), “Dynamics of magnetization at infinite temperature in a Heisenberg spin chain,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adi7877).

title: Thermodynamic stability of one-dimensional many-body localization
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Establish whether generic strongly disordered short-range spin chains remain localized at infinite time and size, and determine when rare thermal inclusions initiate avalanches.
status: Rigorous constructions exist under restrictive assumptions. Avalanche mechanisms leave the stability boundary of widely studied disordered Heisenberg chains contested.
why: Determines whether isolated interacting magnets permanently retain local quantum information.
key_works: Imbrie (2016), “On Many-Body Localization for Quantum Spin Chains,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10955-016-1508-x); De Roeck and Huveneers (2017), “Stability and instability towards delocalization in many-body localization systems,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.95.155129).

title: Avalanche scaling in two-dimensional disordered spin systems
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Establish size and time scaling of avalanche-driven delocalization, including whether any localized phase survives under specified interactions and disorder.
status: A 2025 70-qubit experiment found stronger imbalance decay with increasing size, consistent with delocalization. Asymptotic phase boundaries and avalanche rates remain unresolved.
why: Distinguishes a localization phase from a long transient.
key_works: Li et al. (2025), “Many-body delocalization with a two-dimensional 70-qubit superconducting quantum simulator,” [arXiv:2507.16882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16882).

title: Quasiperiodic many-body-localization criticality
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Determine the thermodynamic transition and critical scaling in interacting quasiperiodic spin chains, including how the absence of conventional random rare regions changes avalanches.
status: Studied since 2013 and observed over finite experimental windows. Transition points and exponents remain sensitive to size, interactions, and modulation.
why: Separates intrinsic localization mechanisms from mechanisms requiring randomness.
key_works: Iyer, Oganesyan, Refael, and Huse (2013), “Many-body localization in a quasiperiodic system,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.87.134202).

title: Long-lived photoinduced chiral spin liquid in a material
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Create a driven material with a chiral-liquid regime lasting longer than equilibration and diagnostic times, while quantifying heating and competing photoinduced states.
status: Floquet theory predicts light-induced chiral interactions; simulators implement related dynamics. A controlled long-lived correlated phase in a solid remains a stronger target.
why: Opens magnetic topological phases unavailable in equilibrium.
key_works: Claassen et al. (2017), “Dynamical time-reversal symmetry breaking and photo-induced chiral spin liquids in frustrated Mott insulators,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-00876-y).
