title: Direct anyon-statistics measurement in a bulk magnetic material
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Measure braiding or interference that distinguishes fractional quasiparticle statistics in an equilibrium magnetic material, excluding ordinary magnon and phonon explanations.
status: Exactly solvable models predict anyons, and quantum processors implement related operations. Candidate-material continua and thermal Hall signals do not directly measure exchange statistics.
why: Provides a decisive test of intrinsic magnetic topological order.
key_works: Kitaev (2006), “Anyons in an exactly solved model and beyond,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005).

title: Disorder-aware entanglement benchmark for magnetic phase diagnosis
subfield: Nonequilibrium quantum magnetism and spin transport
open: Build validated experimentally accessible entanglement benchmarks distinguishing two-dimensional liquids, random singlets, and ordered magnets under realistic disorder and resolution.
status: A 2025 study shows that incorrect disorder averaging can generate false inferences and distinguishes selected one-dimensional states. Realistic two-dimensional discrimination remains incomplete.
why: Prevents entanglement alone from being misidentified as a particular phase.
key_works: Sabharwal, Shimokawa, and Shannon (2025), “Witnessing Disorder in Quantum Magnets,” [arXiv:2407.20797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.20797).

title: Predictive coercivity from real microstructure
open: Predict manufactured magnets’ coercive-field distributions from measured three-dimensional interfaces, defects, temperature, and sweep rate without fitting each specimen’s hysteresis.
status: Brown’s discrepancy dates to the 1940s. Tomographic digital twins reproduced selected Nd–Fe–B samples in 2024; transfer across materials and sizes remains open.
why: Enables quantitative magnet design from processing and structure.
key_works: Bolyachkin et al. (2024), “Tomography-based digital twin of Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01218-5); Brown (1963), *Micromagnetics*.

title: Dy/Tb-free Nd–Fe–B meeting a demanding hot-service envelope
open: Proposed target: manufacture 10-mm-thick Dy/Tb-free parts retaining intrinsic coercivity of at least 1.5 T and remanence of at least 1.0 T at 180 °C after 1,000 hours of aging, at 95% yield.
status: Heavy-rare-earth-free bulk magnets exist. Grain refinement and boundary diffusion improve performance; this combined qualification envelope is a stricter proposed target.
why: Reduces heavy-rare-earth dependence in traction motors.
key_works: Hono and Sepehri-Amin (2012), “Strategy for high-coercivity Nd–Fe–B magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scriptamat.2012.06.038); Gutfleisch et al. (2011), “Magnetic Materials and Devices for the 21st Century: Stronger, Lighter, and More Energy Efficient,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.201002180).

title: Uniform grain-boundary engineering through thick magnets
open: Control boundary chemistry and magnetic isolation throughout centimetre-scale magnets, predicting diffusion depth and the weakest reversal sites from processing.
status: Surface diffusion and core–shell engineering are established. Thin-specimen success does not establish uniform protection of large or complex parts.
why: Makes advanced coercivity treatments useful in large machines.
key_works: Hono and Sepehri-Amin (2012), “Strategy for high-coercivity Nd–Fe–B magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scriptamat.2012.06.038); Bolyachkin et al. (2024), “Tomography-based digital twin of Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01218-5).

title: SmFe12 intrinsic-to-bulk performance gap
open: Stabilize manufacturable ThMn12-type Sm–Fe magnets while retaining high magnetization and anisotropy and generating strong coercivity without excessive stabilizer dilution.
status: An anisotropic sintered magnet reached approximately 1 T coercivity in 2021. Secondary phases and boundary control still separate bulk performance from intrinsic potential.
why: Offers strong magnets with lower rare-earth content.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2021), “Origin of coercivity in an anisotropic Sm(Fe,Ti,V)12-based sintered magnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2021.117161).

title: Dense Sm2Fe17N3 without decomposition
open: Consolidate aligned Sm2Fe17N3 into near-full-density magnets while preserving nitrogen, coercivity, and oxidation resistance through scalable production.
status: Low-temperature compacts exist; dynamic-compression sintering at 473 K was reported in 2024. Combined density, alignment, magnetic performance, and yield remain open.
why: Converts a strong nitride powder into a useful bulk component.
key_works: Saito and Nishio-Hamane (2024), “Structures and magnetic properties of Sm2Fe17N3 bulk magnets prepared by spark plasma sintering with dynamic compression,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2024.172320).

title: High-iron Sm–Co magnets with stable pinning networks
open: Increase magnetization through Fe substitution while retaining reproducible cellular pinning and coercivity throughout prolonged high-temperature service.
status: Sm2Co17-type magnets already serve hot applications. Atomic-scale studies connect chemistry, cellular structure, and pinning, but higher Fe content and lifetime remain coupled constraints.
why: Improves compact magnets for demanding thermal environments.
key_works: Duerrschnabel et al. (2017), “Atomic structure and domain wall pinning in samarium-cobalt-based permanent magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-00059-9).

title: Fast, verifiable bulk tetrataenite synthesis
open: Manufacture predominantly ordered L10 FeNi on industrial timescales, with independent structural verification and useful bulk coercivity.
status: Meteorites establish existence, and induced partial ordering has been reported. A prominent bulk-casting claim was reinterpreted and retracted in 2025 after oxidation-related diffraction artifacts were identified.
why: Could provide a Ni–Fe alternative to rare-earth magnets.
key_works: Lewis and Stamenov (2024), “Accelerating Nature: Induced Atomic Order in Equiatomic FeNi,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202302696); Houghton et al. (2025), “Reinterpretation of Report of Tetrataenite in Bulk Alloy Castings,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202408796).

title: Reproducible intrinsic magnetization of Fe16N2
open: Establish the intrinsic saturation magnetization of α″-Fe16N2 across independent laboratories, separating nitrogen order, strain, phase fractions, and volume-calibration effects.
status: Giant-magnetization claims have persisted for decades. Specimen form and characterization strongly affect results; a 2025 assessment distinguishes exceptional claims from substantiated performance.
why: Determines whether iron nitride has an exceptional intrinsic advantage.
key_works: Dirba et al. (2025), “Fe16N2: Hype, hope, or heavy hitter? A critical review,” [paper](https://magsoc.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/MS_2025_FeN_Hype_or_Heavy_Hitter.pdf).

title: Dense, stable Fe16N2 permanent magnets
open: Consolidate iron-nitride particles into dense aligned magnets without decomposition or oxidation, retaining coercivity through service-temperature cycling.
status: Powders, bonded magnets, and pressure-assisted compacts exist. Thermal instability, oxidation protection, and magnetic dilution remain interacting barriers.
why: Tests whether an abundant-element candidate can become practical.
key_works: Dirba et al. (2025), “Fe16N2: Hype, hope, or heavy hitter? A critical review,” [paper](https://magsoc.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/MS_2025_FeN_Hype_or_Heavy_Hitter.pdf).

title: Defect-controlled coercivity in τ-MnAl
open: Control twins, antiphase boundaries, and decomposition so dense textured τ-MnAl retains magnetization and coercivity after processing.
status: Hard magnetic τ-MnAl is established. Its narrow stability window and reversal-active defects limit bulk performance; a 2025 multiscale study proposes substitutions requiring experimental validation.
why: Develops an inexpensive rare-earth-free magnet family.
key_works: Bhandari et al. (2025), “Enhancing stability, magnetic anisotropy, and coercivity of manganese aluminum: Machine learning, ab initio, and micromagnetic modeling,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.9.034413).

title: MnBi stability–texture–density tradeoff
open: Produce dense aligned MnBi magnets preserving phase purity, oxidation resistance, and favorable elevated-temperature coercivity throughout repeated thermal cycling.
status: Useful powders and bonded magnets exist. Substitution and interface treatments address individual weaknesses without resolving the combined production and lifetime problem.
why: Provides a possible hard magnet for hot environments.
key_works: Enkhtur and Odkhuu (2025), “Atomic engineering of intrinsic permanent magnetism in MnBi,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20764-6).

title: Bulk anisotropic exchange-spring magnets
open: Manufacture dense aligned hard/soft nanocomposites gaining the predicted remanence benefit without soft regions initiating collective reversal.
status: The principle dates to 1991 and works in model structures. Maintaining interface quality and nanometre soft-phase dimensions throughout bulk material remains unresolved.
why: Reduces hard-phase and rare-earth requirements per unit magnetic energy.
key_works: Kneller and Hawig (1991), “The exchange-spring magnet: a new material principle for permanent magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/20.102931); Skomski and Coey (1993), “Giant energy product in nanostructured two-phase magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.48.15812).

title: Alnico draw-annealing mechanism
open: Predict how draw annealing alters reversal in interconnected Fe–Co nanorods, then design treatments approaching alnico’s coercivity potential.
status: Industrially important since the 1930s. Microscopy and atom-probe studies show that chemical refinement alone does not explain the large draw-annealing coercivity increase.
why: Improves an established rare-earth-free magnet through controlled nanostructure.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2018), “On spinodal decomposition in alnico—a transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography study,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2018.04.042); Ke et al. (2017), “Simulation of alnico coercivity,” [arXiv:1707.04180](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04180).

title: High-performance ferrites without La/Co additives
open: Increase abundant-element M-type ferrite energy product through texture, density, and grain boundaries while avoiding dependence on La or Co substitution.
status: Ferrites are mature products. The open target is an improved cost–performance–criticality combination within their intrinsic magnetization limit.
why: Improves the lowest-cost permanent-magnet platform.
key_works: Pullar (2012), “Hexagonal ferrites: A review of the synthesis, properties and applications of hexaferrite ceramics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pmatsci.2012.04.001).

title: Filling the permanent-magnet performance gap
open: Demonstrate a scalable rare-earth-free magnet meeting a proposed 150 kJ/m³ energy-product target at 150 °C, with realistic demagnetization, lifetime, and cost requirements.
status: This is an explicit proposed target. Candidate intermediates between ferrites and rare-earth magnets retain processing or stability limitations.
why: Enables substitution where maximum rare-earth-magnet performance is unnecessary.
key_works: Coey (2012), “Permanent magnets: Plugging the gap,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scriptamat.2012.04.036).

title: Three-dimensional printing of dense anisotropic magnets
open: Print complex, locally oriented magnets approaching dense conventional material performance while controlling alignment, porosity, thermal damage, and dimensional error.
status: Large bonded Nd–Fe–B parts and anisotropic composites have been printed. Binder dilution and process damage still constrain dense high-performance geometries.
why: Enables magnetic circuits difficult to manufacture by cutting and assembly.
key_works: Li et al. (2016), “Big Area Additive Manufacturing of High Performance Bonded NdFeB Magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep36212); Gandha et al. (2018), “Additive manufacturing of anisotropic hybrid NdFeB-SmFeN nylon composite bonded magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2018.07.021).

title: High-induction nanocrystalline cores at megahertz frequencies
open: Combine near-2 T saturation induction with low loss under declared megahertz excitation, DC bias, and operating temperature, retaining economical processing.
status: FINEMET and Fe-rich families supply different combinations of induction and softness. Eddy currents, anisotropy, resistivity, and manufacture remain coupled constraints.
why: Enables smaller inductors and transformers for fast power electronics.
key_works: Yoshizawa, Oguma, and Yamauchi (1988), “New Fe-based soft magnetic alloys composed of ultrafine grain structure,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.342149); Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195).

title: Economical rolling of high-silicon electrical steel
open: Produce thin wide Fe–6.5 wt% Si sheet at high yield and competitive cost while retaining magnetic performance and mechanical integrity.
status: High-silicon sheet and alternative deposition or rapid-solidification routes exist. Ordered-phase embrittlement obstructs inexpensive conventional rolling.
why: Reduces core losses using a well-understood alloy system.
key_works: Ouyang et al. (2019), “Review of Fe-6.5 wt%Si high silicon steel—A promising soft magnetic material for sub-kHz application,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2019.02.089).

title: Softness–strength coexistence in high-induction alloys
open: Design Fe–Co or Fe-rich alloys retaining high saturation and low hysteresis after gaining strength, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability for high-speed rotors.
status: Strengthening changes defects, stress, or phases that also affect domain walls. Existing materials optimize different parts of the property combination.
why: Permits faster lighter machines without sacrificing magnetic efficiency.
key_works: Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195); Coey (2010), *Magnetism and Magnetic Materials*.

title: Thermally stable insulation in soft magnetic composites
open: Develop thin particle coatings surviving compaction and stress-relief annealing without electrical percolation or excessive magnetic dilution.
status: Phosphate, oxide, polymer, and hybrid coatings exist. Stronger compaction and hotter annealing improve some properties while damaging insulation or inducing reactions.
why: Enables efficient three-dimensional cores with lower eddy-current loss.
key_works: Périgo, Weidenfeller, Kollár, and Füzer (2018), “Past, present, and future of soft magnetic composites,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5027045).

title: Long-term stability of nanocrystalline soft magnets
open: Predict and suppress grain growth, stress relaxation, and anisotropy drift over years of combined thermal cycling and mechanical loading.
status: Controlled nanocrystallization and stress annealing yield excellent initial properties. Short annealing tests do not establish service lifetime under coupled stresses.
why: Makes compact hot-running cores reliable in long-lived equipment.
key_works: Herzer (2013), “Modern soft magnets: Amorphous and nanocrystalline materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2012.10.040).

title: Hysteresis loss under arbitrary transient waveforms
open: Predict vector hysteresis and loss during waveform transitions, minor loops, DC-bias changes, and temperature drift with transferable error bounds.
status: Classical loss models and learned models are useful. MagNetX measured transients in 2025; a model generalizing across materials and operating histories remains open.
why: Prevents inefficient or undersized cores in real switching circuits.
key_works: Bertotti (1988), “General properties of power losses in soft ferromagnetic materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/20.43994); Kwon et al. (2025), “MagNetX: Extending the MagNet Database for Modeling Power Magnetics in Transient,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/APEC48143.2025.10977252).

title: Predicting cutting and assembly losses in motor laminations
open: Predict assembled motor-core losses from cutting damage, burrs, joining, clamping, and rotating flux instead of relying on pristine-sheet measurements.
status: Local damage models and manufacturing measurements exist, but their spatial laws and parameters remain process-dependent.
why: Closes the gap between material datasheets and machine efficiency.
key_works: Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195); Bertotti (1988), “General properties of power losses in soft ferromagnetic materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/20.43994).

title: Useful permeability under simultaneous DC bias and heat
open: Design ferrites and powder cores with predictable incremental permeability and low loss under combined DC bias, ripple frequency, and temperature near saturation.
status: Distributed-gap composites and optimized ferrites address parts of the problem. Favorable zero-bias measurements do not establish the combined envelope.
why: Increases usable energy storage in compact inductors.
key_works: Périgo et al. (2018), “Past, present, and future of soft magnetic composites,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5027045); Li et al. (2023), “Why MagNet: Quantifying the Complexity of Modeling Power Magnetic Material Characteristics,” [publication](https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/why-magnet-quantifying-the-complexity-of-modeling-power-magnetic-/).

title: Sharp permeability–bandwidth bounds for structured magnets
open: Derive tight realizable bounds on permeability, bandwidth, loss, and loading for heterogeneous anisotropic spatially dispersive composites under stated passivity assumptions.
status: Snoek-type laws and generalizations exist. Exceeding an isotropic formula by changing assumptions does not settle the optimum for a specified architecture.
why: Separates useful architecture changes from impossible specifications.
key_works: Acher and Dubourg (2008), “Generalization of Snoek’s law to ferromagnetic films and composites,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.77.104440).

title: Tenfold smaller magnetics at unchanged system loss
open: Reduce complete transformer or inductor volume tenfold against a declared baseline while preserving power, efficiency, isolation, temperature rise, lifetime, and electromagnetic compatibility.
status: Proposed system-level moonshot. Higher frequencies and new cores offer routes, but winding, insulation, cooling, and parasitic losses must be counted.
why: Shrinks chargers, converters, and power distribution hardware.
key_works: McHenry, Willard, and Laughlin (1999), “Amorphous and nanocrystalline materials for applications as soft magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0079-6425(99)00002-X); Herzer (2013), “Modern soft magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2012.10.040).

title: Carrier-controlled ferromagnetism above 300 K in (Ba,K)(Zn,Mn)2As2
subfield: Magnetic semiconductors and chiral chemical interfaces
open: Obtain homogeneous material with Curie temperature above 300 K, independently controlling hole density at fixed Mn concentration while preserving semiconducting transport and excluding precipitates.
status: Independent spin and carrier doping was demonstrated in 2013. High-pressure synthesis raised the reported Curie temperature to 260 K in 2025; further Mn strengthened competing antiferromagnetism.
why: Combines ambient-temperature magnetic order with tunable semiconductor carriers.
key_works: Zhao et al. (2013), “New diluted ferromagnetic semiconductor with Curie temperature up to 180 K and isostructural to the ‘122’ iron-based superconductors,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms2447); Peng et al. (2025), “A Near Room Temperature Curie Temperature in a New Type of Diluted Magnetic Semiconductor (Ba,K)(Zn,Mn)2As2,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/apxr.202400124).

title: Microscopic prediction of enantioselective adsorption on ferromagnets
subfield: Magnetic semiconductors and chiral chemical interfaces
open: Predict helicene adsorption-rate ratios on magnetized cobalt under magnetization reversal, temperature changes, and isotope substitution, separating transient spin interactions from equilibrium binding differences.
status: Microscopy established enantioselective adsorption in 2024, while calculations disfavored unequal final binding energies. A 2025 study supports vibration-assisted interactions in another molecular system.
why: Makes magnetic chemical separation predictive.
key_works: Safari et al. (2024), “Enantioselective Adsorption on Magnetic Surfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202308666); Miwa et al. (2025), “Spin polarization driven by molecular vibrations leads to enantioselectivity in chiral molecules,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adv5220).
aliases: Chirality-induced spin selectivity in adsorption; magnetic enantioselection.

title: Granular FePt HAMR write–retention window under grain-size scaling
open: Reduce Curie-temperature dispersion in smaller L10-FePt grains while preserving retention and low write jitter, demonstrating higher recording density under declared heating and field budgets.
status: Commercial HAMR shipped in 2025. A 2025 model attributes approximately 70% of measured Curie-temperature dispersion to grain-size effects; residual dispersion and joint performance remain open.
why: Extends disk density without sacrificing data stability.
key_works: Ochiai et al. (2025), “Anisotropic Exchange Spin Model to Investigate the Curie Temperature Dispersion of Finite-Size L10-FePt Magnetic Nanoparticles,” [arXiv:2502.15247](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.15247).

title: HAMR protection-stack lifetime at tighter head–disk spacing
open: Develop thinner overcoat–lubricant stacks surviving repeated HAMR heating and intermittent contact, with validated lifetime predictions for decomposition, reflow, and debris.
status: Lubricant depletion and recovery were measured in 2024; reactive simulations in 2025 identify shear-driven degradation. Durability at progressively thinner protection remains unresolved.
why: Prevents interface degradation from limiting recording density.
key_works: Cheng et al. (2024), “In-situ sub-angstrom characterization of laser-lubricant interaction in a thermo-tribological system,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44172-024-00284-3); Shekhar et al. (2025), “ReaxFF molecular dynamics study of mechanochemical degradation of PFPE lubricants on DLC in heat-assisted magnetic recording,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5MR00023H).

title: Sub-10-nanometre STT memory with simultaneous retention and writeability
open: Demonstrate sub-10-nanometre spin-transfer-torque junction arrays meeting declared retention, write-error, read-disturb, endurance, and yield requirements simultaneously.
status: Single-digit-nanometre shape-anisotropy switching was demonstrated in 2018. Joint array reliability and current delivery remain unresolved.
why: Extends nonvolatile working memory to smaller dimensions.
key_works: Watanabe et al. (2018), “Shape anisotropy revisited in single-digit nanometer magnetic tunnel junctions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-03003-7).

title: Manufacturable field-free SOT-MRAM operating window
open: Produce dense field-free spin–orbit-torque arrays with deterministic bidirectional switching across process variation, temperature, and aging while meeting selector, current, retention, and readout constraints.
status: Field-free switching and 300-mm-compatible integration were reported by 2019. Competitive simultaneous array metrics remain the target.
why: Enables rapid durable embedded memory without external bias fields.
key_works: Garello et al. (2019), “Manufacturable 300mm platform solution for Field-Free Switching SOT-MRAM,” [arXiv:1907.08012](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.08012); Shao et al. (2021), “Roadmap of spin-orbit torques,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/TMAG.2021.3078583).

title: Predicting magnetic-memory write-error tails from microstructure
open: Predict extremely rare failed or delayed writes from measured defects, thermal fluctuations, and pulse waveforms, validating tails without separately fitted effective temperatures.
status: Single-shot measurements have resolved incubation and reversal stages since 2020. Extrapolation to tiny failure probabilities under production variation remains open.
why: Qualification depends on failures hidden by average switching curves.
key_works: Grimaldi et al. (2020), “Single-shot dynamics of spin–orbit torque and spin transfer torque switching in three-terminal magnetic tunnel junctions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-019-0607-7).

title: Absolute spin-torque metrology across dissimilar interfaces
open: Separately extract bulk spin generation, interfacial transmission, spin-memory loss, and torque absorption using traceable methods agreeing on the same samples.
status: Interfacial spin-memory loss was quantified in 2014. Bulk and interface parameters remain correlated in material-dependent inverse problems.
why: Makes candidate torque-source comparisons meaningful.
key_works: Rojas-Sánchez et al. (2014), “Spin Pumping and Inverse Spin Hall Effect in Platinum: The Essential Role of Spin-Memory Loss at Metallic Interfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.106602).

title: Quantitative orbital-to-spin conversion in light-metal torque devices
open: Determine the orbital contribution to torque, its conversion location, and its dependence on disorder and interface chemistry, then demonstrate lower complete switching energy than matched controls.
status: Long-range orbital transport and large orbital torque were reported in 2023. Transferable efficiencies and manufacturing robustness remain unresolved.
why: Broadens efficient torque materials beyond heavy elements.
key_works: Hayashi et al. (2023), “Observation of long-range orbital transport and giant orbital torque,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42005-023-01139-7).

title: Topological-insulator torque after full device processing
open: Preserve useful spin–charge conversion through deposition, patterning, contacting, and thermal processing, demonstrating reduced complete write energy in an integrated cell.
status: Sputtered bismuth–selenium films showed large room-temperature torque in 2018. Surface contributions, bulk conduction, shunting, and process compatibility remain coupled problems.
why: Tests whether topological states provide a practical memory advantage.
key_works: Mahendra DC et al. (2018), “Room-temperature high spin–orbit torque due to quantum confinement in sputtered BiₓSe₍₁−ₓ₎ films,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0136-z).

title: Timing-tolerant voltage-controlled magnetic switching
open: Achieve deterministic bidirectional voltage-controlled-anisotropy switching over broad pulse-width and temperature windows while retaining nonvolatility and low leakage.
status: Coherent voltage-pulse switching was demonstrated in 2012. Timing sensitivity, thermal dispersion, and retention–anisotropy tradeoffs remain coupled obstacles.
why: Reduces magnetic-writing energy and transistor area.
key_works: Shiota et al. (2012), “Induction of coherent magnetization switching in a few atomic layers of FeCo using voltage pulses,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3172).

title: Scaled sign-resolved collinear-antiferromagnetic memory arrays
open: Combine electrical 180-degree reversal and sign-sensitive electrical readout in dense addressed arrays, quantifying retention, disturbance, endurance, and write-error distributions.
status: CuMnAs reversal and second-order readout were demonstrated in 2018, with no decay observed during 25 hours of probing. Qualified scaled arrays remain open.
why: Turns electrically distinguishable Néel states into reliable dense memory.
key_works: Godinho et al. (2018), “Electrically induced and detected Néel vector reversal in a collinear antiferromagnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-07092-2).

title: Causal attribution of antiferromagnetic electrical switching signals
open: Quantitatively separate Néel-order changes from electromigration, structural relaxation, thermal gradients, and contact drift using simultaneous magnetic probes and matched controls.
status: Nonmagnetic lookalikes were demonstrated in particular devices in 2019. This did not invalidate all antiferromagnetic switching; transferable attribution remains unresolved.
why: Prevents artifacts from becoming accepted switching mechanisms.
key_works: Chiang et al. (2019), “Absence of Evidence of Electrical Switching of the Antiferromagnetic Néel Vector,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.123.227203).

title: Reliable all-antiferromagnetic tunnel-junction memory
open: Demonstrate independently writable all-antiferromagnetic junction arrays retaining resistance contrast, low errors, and endurance after scaling and thermal processing.
status: Octupole-driven spin-torque switching was reported in a 2025 preprint. Domain-dependent torque and tunneling still require reliable integrated operation.
why: Combines antiferromagnetic dynamics with convenient electrical readout.
key_works: Kang et al. (2025), “Octupole-driven spin-transfer torque switching of all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions,” [arXiv:2509.03026v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03026v1).

title: Complete picosecond Mn3Sn memory cycles
open: Integrate picosecond writing with selection, readout, thermal recovery, and interconnect delivery, demonstrating sustained random-access cycles with measured errors and total energy.
status: Switching driven by 40-ps pulses was reported in 2026. Full repeated memory cycles at comparable times remain unresolved.
why: Determines whether antiferromagnetic speed survives circuit overhead.
key_works: Tsai et al. (2026), “Picosecond ultralow-power switching device based on an antiferromagnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adt3136).

title: Fast ferrimagnetic transport over a broad temperature interval
open: Retain compensation-enhanced domain-wall speed and control across useful temperature and composition ranges, rather than near one finely tuned compensation point.
status: Rapid motion near angular-momentum compensation was demonstrated in 2017. Broadening equivalent behavior remains a materials and device challenge.
why: Makes ferrimagnetic transport tolerant of ambient and self-heating fluctuations.
key_works: Kim et al. (2017), “Fast domain wall motion in the vicinity of the angular momentum compensation temperature of ferrimagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat4990).

title: Programmable synchronization of large spin-oscillator networks
open: Independently program frequencies and couplings in large arrays while controlling collective phase despite mismatch and noise, with scaling laws for locking and failure.
status: Long-range mutual synchronization was demonstrated in 2017. Flexible connectivity and predictable operation across heterogeneous arrays remain unresolved.
why: Supports microwave sources, associative memory, and analog optimization.
key_works: Awad et al. (2017), “Long-range mutual synchronization of spin Hall nano-oscillators,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys3927).

title: End-to-end advantage from spin-oscillator learning
open: Demonstrate improved energy, latency, or accuracy against strong digital baselines after including encoding, training, conversion, calibration, and readout, with favorable task-size scaling.
status: Spoken-digit recognition using nanoscale oscillators was demonstrated in 2017. Scalable advantage including surrounding electronics remains unestablished.
why: Identifies workloads benefiting from magnetic nonlinear dynamics.
key_works: Torrejon et al. (2017), “Neuromorphic computing with nanoscale spintronic oscillators,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature23011).

title: Calibrated large-scale magnetic p-bit sampling
open: Build programmable magnetic probabilistic networks with quantified output-distribution error despite correlations, drift, asynchronous timing, and finite mixing.
status: Magnetic-junction factorization appeared in 2019; a 1,143-p-bit integrated computer was reported in 2025. Distributional correctness and useful scaling remain open.
why: Could accelerate sampling, inference, and combinatorial optimization.
key_works: Duffee et al. (2025), “An integrated-circuit-based probabilistic computer that uses voltage-controlled magnetic tunnel junctions as its entropy source,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41928-025-01439-6).

title: Public device-to-algorithm spin-computing benchmark corpus
open: Link raw trajectories, failed devices, fabrication metadata, compact models, peripheral costs, and task outcomes in a versioned reproducible benchmark.
status: The 2026 “Metrics for spin-based computing” review formalizes comparison needs. Existing demonstrations do not constitute a comprehensive interoperable corpus.
why: Exposes hidden costs and supports realistic architecture selection.
key_works: Kurebayashi et al. (2026), “Metrics for spin-based computing,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-025-00918-1).

title: Efficient electrical transduction of exchange-wavelength magnons
open: Electrically launch and detect sub-100-nanometre-wavelength spin waves with calibrated bidirectional efficiency, useful bandwidth, and low complete circuit energy.
status: Approximately 45-nm waves were excited using Co25Fe75 nanowires in 2021. Efficient reciprocal electrical interfaces remain a distinct challenge.
why: Connects nanoscale magnon channels to electronics.
key_works: Wang et al. (2021), “Sub-50 nm wavelength spin waves excited by low-damping Co25Fe75 nanowires,” [Applied Physics Letters 119, 152402](https://pubs.aip.org/aip/apl/article-abstract/119/15/152402/40480/Sub-50-nm-wavelength-spin-waves-excited-by-low).

title: Deep magnonic logic with fan-out and controlled error accumulation
open: Operate many successive logic stages with electrical input/output, fan-out, specified noise margins, and bounded accumulated errors, counting restoration and routing energy.
status: A 2026 preprint reports phase-independent nonlinear restoration and deterministic multistage logic. Deep fully interfaced circuit reliability remains open.
why: Determines whether spin-wave logic can scale into processors.
key_works: Guo et al. (2026), “Integrated magnonic chip using cascaded logic,” [arXiv:2601.02644](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02644).

title: Foundry-compatible low-damping patterned garnet films
open: Combine low damping, nanoscale patterning, compatible substrates, and semiconductor thermal budgets across a wafer, measuring degradation after complete fabrication.
status: Damping near 8.6 × 10⁻⁵ in 22-nm YIG was reported in 2014, a historical milestone. Integration remains an explicit concern in the 2024 roadmap.
why: Bridges excellent laboratory films and scalable circuits.
key_works: Chang et al. (2014), “Nanometer-Thick Yttrium Iron Garnet Films With Extremely Low Damping,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/LMAG.2014.2350958); Flebus et al. (2024), “The 2024 magnonics roadmap,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-648X/ad399c).

title: Broadband low-loss nonreciprocal magnon routing
open: Build programmable isolators or circulators retaining directional contrast across useful bandwidth and power while minimizing insertion loss and bias overhead.
status: Chiral coupling and microwave-isolation demonstrations exist, including bound magnonic-polariton states in 2023. Broadband cascadable routing remains unresolved.
why: Controls reflections and back-action in dense wave circuits.
key_works: Han et al. (2023), “Bound chiral magnonic polariton states for ideal microwave isolation,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adg4730).

title: Universality of phase ordering in finite-lifetime magnon condensates
open: Determine scaling laws for spontaneous phase ordering, coherence growth, vortices, and defect annihilation in driven magnon condensates with finite lifetime.
status: Room-temperature condensation was reported in 2006; spontaneous phase coherence was directly resolved in 2026. Dynamics and universality remain the questions.
why: Tests statistical mechanics of open quantum fluids.
key_works: Koster et al. (2026), “Emergence of phase coherence in a magnon Bose–Einstein condensate,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03373-6).

title: Unambiguous electrically controlled antiferromagnetic spin superfluidity
open: Demonstrate transport governed by a controlled coherent phase gradient or winding, with phase-sensitive evidence excluding diffusive magnons and heating, and measured phase-slip rates.
status: Long-distance transport through antiferromagnetic iron oxide was demonstrated in 2018. Propagation distance alone does not establish superfluidity.
why: Could enable low-dissipation angular-momentum interconnects.
key_works: Lebrun et al. (2018), “Tunable long-distance spin transport in a crystalline antiferromagnetic iron oxide,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0490-7).

title: Distributed single-magnon quantum circuits
open: Transfer, store, and retrieve nonclassical magnon states between independently addressable nodes while preserving measured coherence or entanglement.
status: Entanglement-based single-shot detection of one magnon was demonstrated in 2020. Distributed architectures still need tunable coupling, low loss, and scalable integration.
why: Adds magnetic memories and transducers to modular quantum systems.
key_works: Lachance-Quirion et al. (2020), “Entanglement-based single-shot detection of a single magnon with a superconducting qubit,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaz9236); Serha et al. (2025), “Magnetic Materials for Quantum Magnonics,” [arXiv:2510.09331](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09331).

title: Quantum-efficient magnon microwave–optical conversion
open: Demonstrate bidirectional conversion with efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth sufficient to preserve nonclassical states, suppressing optical heating in the same device.
status: Conversion was demonstrated in 2016; a 2026 CrSBr preprint reports broadband magnon–exciton transduction. Classical coherence does not establish quantum suitability.
why: Connects microwave quantum processors to optical networks.
key_works: Hisatomi et al. (2016), “Bidirectional conversion between microwave and light via ferromagnetic magnons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.93.174427); Adak et al. (2026), “Microwave-to-optical transduction using magnon-exciton coupling in a layered antiferromagnet,” [arXiv:2604.03441](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03441).

title: Useful topological magnon edge channels with damping and interactions
open: Demonstrate a topological edge channel retaining measurable transport advantages under disorder, temperature, nonlinear scattering, and realistic damping, with verified failure boundaries.
status: Topological magnon bands are established research territory. Band topology alone does not guarantee long-lived electrically usable edge information transport.
why: Tests whether topology improves practical wave transport.
key_works: McClarty (2022), “Topological Magnons: A Review,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031620-104715).

title: Local tomography of nonequilibrium magnon distributions
open: Reconstruct frequency-, position-, and time-dependent magnon occupations beyond one effective temperature or chemical potential, calibrating back-action against independent currents.
status: NV magnetometry measured a local spin chemical potential in 2017. Strongly nonthermal distributions remain incompletely observable.
why: Supplies missing inputs for quantitative transport and heating models.
key_works: Du et al. (2017), “Control and local measurement of the spin chemical potential in a magnetic insulator,” [arXiv:1611.07408](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07408).

title: Predictive multireservoir theory of the spin Seebeck effect
open: Predict spin-Seebeck signals across temperature, thickness, frequency, and interfaces using independently determined electron, magnon, phonon, and boundary parameters.
status: Multiple limiting descriptions are successful. A transferable theory identifying where local temperatures fail or mode-selective transport dominates remains open.
why: Enables rational thermal spin-current design.
key_works: Bauer, Saitoh, and van Wees (2012), “Spin caloritronics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3301).

title: Tenfold practical improvement in spin-Seebeck heat harvesting
open: Proposed moonshot: increase useful electrical power tenfold against a reproducible module baseline at fixed footprint and thermal conditions, counting all thermal and electrical parasitics.
status: Spin-Seebeck generation is demonstrated. Materials advances and voltage increases do not by themselves establish improved useful conversion efficiency.
why: Could enable conformal harvesters on difficult geometries.
key_works: Uchida and Hirai (2026), “Spin caloritronics: History and future prospects of experiments,” [arXiv:2605.01692](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01692).

title: Net refrigeration from the spin Peltier effect
open: Demonstrate removal of a calibrated useful heat load after accounting for Joule heating, thermal shunts, and drive electronics, establishing coefficient of performance.
status: The spin Peltier effect was observed in magnetic-insulator structures in 2014. Useful net refrigeration remains a more demanding target.
why: Tests whether spin-mediated heat control becomes practical cooling.
key_works: Flipse et al. (2014), “Observation of the spin Peltier effect,” [arXiv:1311.4772](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4772).

title: Traceable interlaboratory spin-caloritronic datasets
open: Establish reference samples, thermal maps, heat-flux calibration, contact protocols, and uncertainty budgets in a reusable multi-laboratory dataset.
status: A five-laboratory round robin in 2019 found substantial differences and assessed heat-flux normalization. It does not supply a universal standard.
why: Makes conversion coefficients and screening results comparable.
key_works: Sola et al. (2019), “Spincaloritronic Measurements: A Round Robin Comparison of the Longitudinal Spin Seebeck Effect,” [arXiv:1812.00999](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.00999).

title: Complete femtosecond angular-momentum accounting
open: Close the time-resolved angular-momentum budget during demagnetization by measuring spin, electronic orbital motion, lattice motion, and transport with compatible absolute calibrations.
status: Ultrafast demagnetization was observed in 1996. Direct lattice-transfer evidence appeared in 2019; a complete sub-100-fs multichannel budget remains missing.
why: Identifies physical speed and dissipation limits.
key_works: Dornes et al. (2019), “The ultrafast Einstein–de Haas effect,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0822-7).

title: Parameter-predictive ultrafast demagnetization theory
open: Predict demagnetization across materials, thicknesses, excitations, and interfaces using independently constrained inputs rather than retuned phenomenological rates.
status: Several mechanisms explain important regimes since the 1996 nickel experiment. Their quantitative partition and transferability remain unresolved.
why: Converts empirical ultrafast optimization into predictive design.
key_works: Beaurepaire et al. (1996), “Ultrafast Spin Dynamics in Ferromagnetic Nickel,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.4250); Battiato et al. (2010), “Superdiffusive Spin Transport as a Mechanism of Ultrafast Demagnetization,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.105.027203).

title: Predictive materials rule for single-pulse all-optical reversal
open: Derive a transferable criterion predicting deterministic switching windows from exchange, damping, sublattice moments, absorption, and heat flow.
status: Transient ferromagnetic-like alignment during reversal was measured in 2011. Existing mechanisms do not yet constitute a general quantitative discovery rule.
why: Broadens fast optical memory materials beyond empirical composition searches.
key_works: Radu et al. (2011), “Transient ferromagnetic-like state mediating ultrafast reversal of antiferromagnetically coupled spins,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09901).

title: Dense direct-overwrite optical magnetic arrays
open: Write either desired state directly into selected nanoscale cells without first reading them, avoiding neighboring optical and thermal disturbance and measuring array error distributions.
status: Helicity-dependent switching and spintronic integration are established. Dense selective repeatable overwrite imposes stricter requirements than isolated demonstrations.
why: Connects femtosecond control to random-access storage.
key_works: Mangin et al. (2014), “Engineered materials for all-optical helicity-dependent magnetic switching,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3864); Lalieu et al. (2019), “Integrating all-optical switching with spintronics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-08062-4).

title: Rare-earth-free optically written tunnel-junction memory
open: Integrate rare-earth-free single-pulse switching with useful tunneling contrast, retention, low errors, and process compatibility over a broad fluence and temperature window.
status: Gadolinium-free Mn2RuxGa toggle switching was demonstrated in 2020. The joint memory-cell requirements remain unresolved.
why: Broadens optical-memory materials and supply options.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2020), “Single pulse all-optical toggle switching of magnetization without gadolinium in the ferrimagnet Mn2RuxGa,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-18340-9).

title: Sustained gigahertz all-optical magnetic writing
open: Demonstrate long sequences of independently chosen writes at gigahertz rates with measured errors, retention, endurance, and steady-state thermal control.
status: Two-shot experiments in 2021 achieved roughly 300-ps pulse separation. Paired-event recovery does not establish sustained random-access array operation.
why: Determines whether ultrafast switching yields sustained throughput.
key_works: Wang et al. (2021), “Dual-shot dynamics and ultimate frequency of all-optical magnetic recording on GdFeCo,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-020-00451-z).

title: Low-heating, lasting optical reprogramming of exchange
open: Reversibly change exchange or magnetic order beyond the pulse duration with bounded unwanted heating, distinguishing coherent control from thermal alteration.
status: Theory advanced in 2015; light-driven-phonon control was demonstrated in 2021. Durable, efficient repeated programming remains open.
why: Enables magnetic functions unavailable through static fields.
key_works: Mentink, Balzer, and Eckstein (2015), “Ultrafast and reversible control of the exchange interaction in Mott insulators,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms7708); Afanasiev et al. (2021), “Ultrafast control of magnetic interactions via light-driven phonons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-021-00922-7).

title: On-chip coherent terahertz antiferromagnetic switching
open: Integrate a terahertz source, magnetic element, and readout providing deterministic low-error reorientation with useful total energy and recovery time.
status: Coherent terahertz control was demonstrated in 2011, with later switching in selected orthoferrites. Complete miniaturized devices remain unresolved.
why: Converts exchange-scale dynamics into compact ultrafast functionality.
key_works: Kampfrath et al. (2011), “Coherent terahertz control of antiferromagnetic spin waves,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2010.259); Afanasiev (2026), “From equilibrium to ultrafast antiferromagnetism,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02686-4).

title: Microscopic origin and universality of magnetic inertia
open: Predict magnetic memory kernels and nutation from electronic structure and scattering, separating genuine inertia from mode interference and excitation artifacts.
status: Ferromagnetic nutation near 0.6 THz was reported in 2021. Its microscopic coefficient and range of validity remain unresolved.
why: Establishes the equations governing subpicosecond control.
key_works: Neeraj et al. (2021), “Inertial spin dynamics in ferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-020-01040-y).

title: Efficient programmable integrated spintronic terahertz emitters
open: Improve complete electrical-to-optical-to-terahertz efficiency while preserving bandwidth, emitted field, polarization control, and reliability, including the pump system.
status: Efficient ultrabroadband metallic emitters were demonstrated in 2016. Favorable film conversion does not establish efficient compact sources.
why: Supplies adaptable terahertz imaging, spectroscopy, and communication tools.
key_works: Seifert et al. (2016), “Efficient metallic spintronic emitters of ultrabroadband terahertz radiation,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2016.91).

title: Stable mobile sub-10-nanometre room-temperature skyrmions
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Proposed size target: realize sub-10-nanometre skyrmions at room temperature and zero applied field with measured retention, reliable writing, and controllable motion in one platform.
status: Sub-20-nanometre zero-field room-temperature skyrmions were reported in 2026. Size alone does not solve stability, mobility, and readout together.
why: Could enable very-high-density topological storage.
key_works: Darwin et al. (2026), “Bias-Engineered Synthetic Antiferromagnets Hosting Sub-20 nm Zero-Field Skyrmions at Room Temperature,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.75825).

title: Low-error single-skyrmion writing and erasure
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Create or delete exactly one skyrmion at a selected site with measured low failure probability, minimal neighbor disturbance, and reproducible energy across cycling.
status: Deterministic generation and guiding through ion-modified regions were demonstrated in 2022. Array fidelity, endurance, and operating margin remain open.
why: Supplies a reliable elementary texture-memory operation.
key_works: Kern et al. (2022), “Deterministic Generation and Guided Motion of Magnetic Skyrmions by Focused He+-Ion Irradiation,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.2c00670).

title: Error-certified transport of dense skyrmion trains
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Move long closely spaced trains through realistic tracks with bounded annihilation, duplication, pinning, overtaking, and timing errors.
status: Individual motion and guided trains exist. Stochastic racetrack dynamics remain active research in 2026; complete accumulated error rates are unresolved.
why: Converts single-texture motion into dependable shift-register operation.
key_works: Hlushchenko et al. (2026), “Stochastic dynamics of skyrmions on a racetrack: Impact of equilibrium and nonequilibrium noise,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/73z4-ymkp); Koraltan et al. (2026), “The 2026 Skyrmionics Roadmap,” [arXiv:2601.16575](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16575).

title: Fast nondestructive electrical readout of nanoscale skyrmions
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Electrically identify one small skyrmion at useful latency with calibrated signal-to-noise, energy, and disturbance, distinguishing occupancy from size fluctuations.
status: Single sub-100-nanometre room-temperature skyrmions were electrically detected in 2018. Scaled high-bandwidth operation remains unresolved.
why: Connects texture storage to conventional electronics.
key_works: Maccariello et al. (2018), “Electrical detection of single magnetic skyrmions in metallic multilayers at room temperature,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-017-0044-4).

title: Predictive skyrmion lifetimes in disordered devices
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Predict absolute lifetimes and escape pathways in patterned films with defects, edges, and nonuniform interactions without arbitrary fitted attempt frequencies.
status: Atomistic calculations established collapse and boundary escape in 2018. Mapping measured disorder to device lifetime distributions remains open.
why: Distinguishes topology from practical retention.
key_works: Bessarab et al. (2018), “Lifetime of racetrack skyrmions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-21623-3).

title: Robust skyrmion Hall suppression away from perfect compensation
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Maintain negligible transverse drift despite layer imbalance, gradients, defects, deformation, and high drive, establishing tolerances before edge loss or decoupling.
status: Synthetic-antiferromagnetic skyrmions reached approximately 900 m/s with suppressed Hall motion in 2024. Broad operating robustness remains open.
why: Enables narrow fast racetracks with fewer boundary losses.
key_works: Pham et al. (2024), “Fast current-induced skyrmion motion in synthetic antiferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add5751).

title: Identifiable topological Hall signatures
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Quantitatively isolate real-space topological Hall transport from multichannel anomalous Hall effects, inhomogeneity, and momentum-space Berry curvature using simultaneous texture measurements.
status: A 2018 analysis demonstrated nontopological explanations for common Hall features. Hall humps alone remain insufficient texture evidence.
why: Makes electrical texture identification reproducible and falsifiable.
key_works: Gerber (2018), “Interpretation of experimental evidence of the topological Hall effect,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.98.214440).

title: Addressable hopfion writing, transport, and readout
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Reversibly create, move, and electrically distinguish individual hopfions while verifying three-dimensional topology and lifetime throughout manipulation.
status: Creation and observation were reported in 2021; laser nucleation followed in 2026. Integrated repeatable manipulation and readout remain open.
why: Tests three-dimensional topological information carriers.
key_works: Kent et al. (2021), “Creation and observation of Hopfions in magnetic multilayer systems,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-21846-5); Zheng et al. (2026), “Laser-induced nucleation of magnetic hopfions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03236-0).

title: Reliable room-temperature antiskyrmion steering
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Demonstrate programmable motion and routing with controlled anisotropic Hall response, low edge loss, and stability without continuous external-field support.
status: Above-room-temperature antiskyrmions were observed in tetragonal Heuslers in 2017. Reliable device creation, steering, and reading remain separate targets.
why: Uses anisotropic topology for directional information processing.
key_works: Nayak et al. (2017), “Magnetic antiskyrmions above room temperature in tetragonal Heusler materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature23466).

title: Scalable arbitrary microstate programming in artificial spin ice
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Write arbitrary physically allowed configurations in large arrays with local selectivity, speed, and measured errors while retaining controlled interactions.
status: Reconfigurable spectra and mode hybridization were demonstrated in 2021. Global reconfiguration does not supply efficient arbitrary site-by-site programming.
why: Enables programmable wave media and selected frustrated states.
key_works: Gartside et al. (2021), “Reconfigurable magnonic mode-hybridisation and spectral control in a bicomponent artificial spin ice,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22723-x).

title: Equilibrated three-dimensional artificial spin ice
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Build a three-dimensional lattice that thermally explores relevant configurations and allows full spin-state measurement, establishing bulk Coulomb behavior and monopole kinetics.
status: Frustrated three-dimensional nanowire lattices were fabricated in 2019. Equilibration and bulk-resolved statistical mechanics remain substantially harder.
why: Creates controllable experiments on emergent gauge fields.
key_works: May et al. (2019), “Realisation of a frustrated 3D magnetic nanowire lattice,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42005-018-0104-6).

title: Reproducible useful computation with artificial-spin-ice reservoirs
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Demonstrate task scaling and generalization across independently fabricated arrays while counting initialization, training, instrumentation, and readout energy.
status: Training and reservoir computing in spin-vortex ice were demonstrated in 2022. Scalable advantage over suitable baselines remains unestablished.
why: Tests whether many-body magnetic dynamics offer practical computation.
key_works: Gartside et al. (2022), “Reconfigurable training and reservoir computing in an artificial spin-vortex ice via spin-wave fingerprinting,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-022-01091-7).

title: Wafer-scale ambient-stable room-temperature ultrathin magnets
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Grow uniform room-temperature monolayer or few-layer magnetic films surviving ambient handling and complete processing with reproducible anisotropy, switching, and wafer yield.
status: Monolayer order was established in 2017; Fe3GaTe2 showed above-room-temperature ferromagnetism in 2022. Growth, stability, and integration remain joint constraints.
why: Supplies practical atomically thin magnetic building blocks.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2022), “Above-room-temperature strong intrinsic ferromagnetism in 2D van der Waals Fe3GaTe2 with large perpendicular magnetic anisotropy,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32605-5).

title: Reconciliation of monolayer VSe2 magnetism
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Establish a reproducible phase map linking magnetic signals to substrate, stoichiometry, defects, strain, and charge-density-wave order, identifying intrinsic versus reconstructed phases.
status: Room-temperature ferromagnetism was reported in 2018; subsequent work found charge-density-wave suppression of ferromagnetism. Sample-dependent outcomes remain incompletely reconciled.
why: Resolves a prominent materials-identification controversy.
key_works: Bonilla et al. (2018), “Strong room-temperature ferromagnetism in VSe2 monolayers on van der Waals substrates,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-018-0063-9); Fumega et al. (2019), “Absence of Ferromagnetism in VSe2 Caused by Its Charge Density Wave Phase,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.9b08868).

title: Fast purely electrostatic control of two-dimensional magnetism
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Reversibly control a useful magnetic state with a solid-state gate at practical speed while excluding ion migration, chemical reactions, and irreversible defects.
status: Gate-tunable room-temperature Fe3GeTe2 ferromagnetism was demonstrated in 2018. Fast chemically unambiguous operation across repeated processing-compatible devices remains open.
why: Connects magnetic functions to low-charge electronic control.
key_works: Deng et al. (2018), “Gate-tunable room-temperature ferromagnetism in two-dimensional Fe3GeTe2,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0626-9).

title: Inverse design of moiré magnetic textures
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Predict texture and magnon spectrum from measured twist, relaxation, strain, and stacking, then reproducibly fabricate a requested pattern with quantified tolerances.
status: Coexisting ferro- and antiferromagnetic regions in twisted CrI3 were demonstrated in 2022. Predictable fabrication of specified patterns remains open.
why: Enables designer magnetic superlattices and wave networks.
key_works: Xu et al. (2022), “Coexisting ferromagnetic–antiferromagnetic state in twisted bilayer CrI3,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-021-01014-y).

title: Practical-temperature van der Waals spin-filter junctions
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Retain large tunneling contrast at useful temperature and bias while demonstrating writing, endurance, and yield in integrated devices.
status: Giant spin-filter magnetoresistance was demonstrated in 2018, prominently in cryogenic CrI3. Simultaneous high-temperature memory performance remains unresolved.
why: Exploits atomically sharp barriers for memory and spin selection.
key_works: Song et al. (2018), “Giant tunneling magnetoresistance in spin-filter van der Waals heterostructures,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aar4851).

title: Independently controlled graphene magnetic-proximity spin circuits
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Combine tunable proximity exchange, efficient injection, long-distance transport, and independent readout while separating exchange control from contact and carrier changes.
status: Graphene–CrSBr spin generation was demonstrated in 2021; tunable polarization followed in 2024. Fully controlled scalable circuits remain open.
why: Adds magnetic functionality to graphene transport channels.
key_works: Ghiasi et al. (2021), “Electrical and thermal generation of spin currents by magnetic bilayer graphene,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-021-00887-3); Yang et al. (2024), “Electrostatically controlled spin polarization in Graphene-CrSBr magnetic proximity heterostructures,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-48809-w).

title: Integrated exciton–magnon magnetic photonics
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Build an integrated optical modulator or coherent processing element with measured loss, modulation depth, bandwidth, and drive energy, preserving coupling after patterning.
status: Coherent exciton-coupled magnons in CrSBr were demonstrated in 2022. Coupling alone does not establish a competitive photonic function.
why: Connects magnetic dynamics directly to strong optical resonances.
key_works: Bae et al. (2022), “Exciton-coupled coherent magnons in a 2D semiconductor,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05024-1).

title: Sample-resolved magnetic phase identification in RuO2
open: Determine whether reproducible compositions, strain states, defects, or interfaces host altermagnetic order, reconciling positive interpretations with direct null measurements.
status: RuO2 remains contested: 2024 μSR/neutron and 2025 bulk quantum-oscillation work support nonmagnetic interpretations. This does not negate established altermagnetism elsewhere.
why: Separates a sample-dependent controversy from the broader symmetry class.
key_works: Keßler et al. (2024), “Absence of magnetic order in RuO2: insights from μSR spectroscopy and neutron diffraction,” [arXiv:2405.10820](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10820); Qian et al. (2025), “Determining the Nature of Magnetism in Altermagnetic Candidate RuO2,” [arXiv:2504.21138](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21138).

title: Reliable all-electrical altermagnetic memory
open: Integrate independently verified order reversal and robust readout with low errors, retention, and endurance, establishing tolerance to domain and orientation variation.
status: Symmetry engineering enabled electrical manipulation and a field-free mode in CrSb in 2025. Qualified nanoscale memory remains the target.
why: Tests fast compensated spin-split materials as useful electronics.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), “Manipulation of the altermagnetic order in CrSb via crystal symmetry,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08436-3); Jungwirth et al. (2026), “Altermagnetic spintronics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03337-w).

title: Absolute nonrelativistic spin-splitter efficiency
open: Measure altermagnetic spin-current magnitude and angular structure while separating spin–orbit, thermal, interfacial, and parasitic magnetic contributions.
status: Efficient nonrelativistic splitting was proposed in 2021, and band splitting has been observed. Band structure alone does not establish usable conversion efficiency.
why: Tests a distinct potentially efficient spin-source mechanism.
key_works: González-Hernández et al. (2021), “Efficient Electrical Spin Splitter Based on Nonrelativistic Collinear Antiferromagnetism,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127701).

title: Finite-temperature interacting altermagnetic spectra
open: Predict and verify temperature-dependent splitting, linewidths, and transport in established altermagnets, connecting correlations and scattering to actual spin-current lifetimes.
status: Splitting was measured in MnTe and CrSb in 2024. A 2026 model establishes spin-dependent lifetimes; quantitative real-material predictions remain open.
why: Determines the operating window for useful spin polarization.
key_works: Krempaský et al. (2024), “Altermagnetic lifting of Kramers spin degeneracy,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06907-7); Leraand et al. (2026), “Spin-dependent quasiparticle lifetimes in altermagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/r3vm-m1m3).

title: Altermagnetic classification in locally distorted real crystals
open: Determine which symmetry-derived properties survive local distortions, defects, twinning, and domains, and develop experimentally usable classification criteria.
status: The framework was organized in 2022; a 2026 preprint reports local symmetry breaking in MnTe. Average crystallography may miss relevant structure.
why: Connects ideal symmetry labels to reproducible material behavior.
key_works: Šmejkal, Sinova, and Jungwirth (2022), “Emerging Research Landscape of Altermagnetism,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.12.040501); Ren et al. (2026), “Atomic-Scale Observation of Symmetry Breaking in Altermagnetic MnTe,” [arXiv:2605.27543](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27543).

title: Electrically routed chiral magnons in altermagnets
open: Electrically generate, select, route, and detect opposite magnon chiralities with quantified losses and crosstalk, reconfiguring without large external fields.
status: A 2026 preprint reports polarized-neutron observation of switchable chiral magnons in MnTe. Electrical transport and routing remain open.
why: Enables polarization-encoded information in compensated magnets.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), “Observation of Switchable Chiral Magnons in an Altermagnet,” [arXiv:2605.14124](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14124).

title: Strong, switchable room-temperature single-phase multiferroics
open: Find a stable insulating phase combining substantial spontaneous magnetization, switchable polarization, and reproducible electric magnetization reversal above 300 K, excluding secondary phases.
status: Pursued for decades. BiFeO3, engineered ferrites, and heterostructures establish important components; large moments, low leakage, and practical switching remain difficult together.
why: Enables compact electrically written magnetic elements.
key_works: Spaldin and Ramesh (2019), “Advances in magnetoelectric multiferroics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0275-2); Yu (2025), “Revolutions of multiferroic materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44306-025-00077-0).

title: Defect-tolerant deterministic magnetoelectric reversal
open: Predict and control nanoscale switching despite defects, domain multiplicity, and cycling, demonstrating low array error rates and retention after removing writing fields.
status: Deterministic electric reversal at room temperature was demonstrated in 2014. Reliable array-level behavior remains a distinct challenge.
why: Converts microscopic coupling into reproducible components.
key_works: Heron et al. (2014), “Deterministic switching of ferromagnetism at room temperature using an electric field,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14004).

title: Ultrathin multiferroic retention beyond a structural snapshot
open: Determine thickness, boundary, and defect conditions for useful retention and repeated switching of both electric and magnetic states in ultrathin BiFeO3.
status: A 2023 study examined coexistence and cycloid suppression near 1.4 nm. Patterned-device behavior and retained coupled order remain unresolved.
why: Establishes realistic multiferroic scaling limits.
key_works: Dufour et al. (2023), “Onset of Multiferroicity in Prototypical Single-Spin Cycloid BiFeO3 Thin Films,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.3c02875).

title: Large-polarization spin-driven multiferroics above room temperature
open: Identify a spin-driven multiferroic combining robust ordering above room temperature, substantial reversible polarization, and small control fields.
status: Spin-induced polarization has been studied since the early 2000s; room-temperature examples exist. The combined polarization, field, temperature, and hysteresis requirements remain restrictive.
why: Makes intrinsically strong coupling useful under ordinary conditions.
key_works: Mostovoy (2024), “Multiferroics: different routes to magnetoelectric coupling,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44306-024-00021-8).

title: Practical four-state ferrotoroidic materials
open: Independently write, read, and retain ferrotoroidic domain states at room temperature with feasible fields, preserving four-state operation in films and repeated cycles.
status: Preferential selection of four domains in LiNi0.8Fe0.2PO4 was demonstrated in 2026. The cryogenic bulk result leaves practical-temperature operation open.
why: Adds controllable magnetic state variables for memory.
key_works: Qureshi et al. (2026), “Toroidicity as a route towards non-volatile quaternary memory in antiferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70767-8).

title: Switchable polarity in metallic ferromagnets
open: Establish reversible electric-field control of polar distortion in a ferromagnetic metal, separating structural switching from charging, ion migration, heating, and current torques.
status: Designed polar ferromagnetic metals appeared in 2024; current-driven magnetic switching followed in 2026. Neither alone proves reversal of polar distortion.
why: Connects metallic transport to controllable structural symmetry.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2024), “A correlated ferromagnetic polar metal by design,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01856-6); Shi et al. (2026), “A Ferromagnetic Polar Metal With Efficient Electrical Switch of Magnetism,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.74269).

title: Cycling-stable strain transfer across magnetoelectric interfaces
open: Predict and suppress interfacial slip, cracking, ferroelastic rearrangement, and stress-induced loss of magnetoelectric response through specified operating cycles.
status: Large strain-mediated coupling is established. Interface and fabrication control remain prominent constraints in 2024 assessments; initial peak response does not establish lifetime.
why: Enables durable sensors, transducers, and voltage-controlled components.
key_works: Taniyama, Gohda, Hamaya, and Kimura (2024), “Artificial multiferroic heterostructures—electric field effects and their perspectives,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/14686996.2024.2412970).

title: Low-frequency noise limits of lead-free magnetoelectric sensors
open: Establish validated sensitivity–bandwidth–size limits below 100 Hz including magnetic noise, vibration, drift, and packaging, identifying improvements that preserve bandwidth.
status: Lead-free laminates exist; electrode design and annealing improved quartz/Metglas sensors in 2024. Packaged broadband performance remains harder than resonant sensitivity.
why: Enables compact low-power sensing outside controlled laboratories.
key_works: Sun et al. (2024), “Reducing equivalent magnetic noise by electrode design and magnetic annealing in Quartz/Metglas magnetoelectric sensors,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sna.2024.115903).

title: Proton-driven magnetism with joint speed, retention, and endurance
open: Demonstrate rapid proton-gated switching, nonvolatile retention, and long cycling lifetime together under controlled humidity and temperature.
status: Solid-state proton pumps enabled reversible room-temperature anisotropy control in 2018–2019. Faster transport can increase spontaneous state drift.
why: Enables low-voltage magnetic reconfiguration.
key_works: Tan et al. (2019), “Magneto-ionic control of magnetism using a solid-state proton pump,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0211-5).

title: Magneto-ionic cycling without irreversible redox damage
open: Identify oxygen reservoirs and diffusion paths restoring the same magnetic microstructure over extended cycling, tracking chemistry and morphology alongside average magnetization.
status: Reversible oxygen-mediated anisotropy modulation exists, including crystallized CoFeB/MgO work in 2025. Apparent magnetic reversibility does not exclude cumulative damage.
why: Establishes defensible lifetimes for electrically reconfigurable magnets.
key_works: Chen et al. (2025), “Reversible magneto ionics in crystallized W Co20Fe60B20 MgO HfO2 ultra-thin films with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy,” [arXiv:2502.18248](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18248).

title: Selective control of multiple mobile ions
open: Independently address different ionic species to obtain predictable reversible magnetic states without segregation, using a validated coupled transport-and-redox model.
status: Boron/iron/oxygen and carbon/iron transport were reported in 2025. General independent species control remains unresolved.
why: Supplies multiple chemical control variables for programmable magnets.
key_works: Ma et al. (2025), “Charge-transfer-mediated boron magneto-ionics: Towards voltage-driven multi-ion transport,” [arXiv:2503.11405](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11405); Tan et al. (2025), “Carbon magneto-ionics: Control of magnetism through voltage-driven carbon transport,” [arXiv:2503.11337](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11337).

title: Room-temperature all-nitride magneto-ionic phase control
open: Reversibly control antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic nitride phases at room temperature with retention and endurance, accounting for nitrogen and excluding oxidation.
status: A manganese-nitride platform showed reversible magnetic and exchange-bias changes in 2025, with highlighted magnetic measurements at 5 K. The practical-temperature package remains open.
why: Broadens ionic magnetic control beyond oxides.
key_works: Chen et al. (2025), “Reconfigurable All-Nitride Magneto-Ionics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.5c04013).

title: Large reversible caloric changes without transition hysteresis
open: Preserve large entropy and temperature changes while reducing hysteresis enough for repeated low-field operation, optimizing actual reversible cycles.
status: Central since the 1997 giant-magnetocaloric discoveries. Compatibility engineering and alloying reduce losses, but large first-sweep responses need not maximize refrigeration.
why: Determines cooling efficiency and field requirements.
key_works: Gutfleisch et al. (2016), “Mastering hysteresis in magnetocaloric materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2015.0308).

title: Magnetocaloric fatigue under realistic thermal-fluid loading
open: Predict and prevent cracking, pulverization, and caloric degradation over service cycles with coolant flow and thermal gradients, validating accelerated tests.
status: Brittle first-order materials remain vulnerable. Flexible La(Fe,Si)13/polymer mats improved processing and bending in 2024 without establishing full thermomagnetic lifetime.
why: Prevents declining cooling and coolant contamination.
key_works: Bayzi Isfahani et al. (2024), “Flexible Magnetocaloric Fiber Mats for Room-Temperature Energy Applications,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.3c15833).

title: Corrosion protection that survives magnetic breathing
open: Protect regenerators throughout their lifetime without obstructing channels or heat flow, including coating defects, coolant changes, and magnetovolume cycling.
status: Copper coatings and tailored inhibitors enabled stable LaFeSi regenerator operation in 2025. Robustness across production variation and lifetime histories remains unresolved.
why: Makes efficient aqueous heat exchange compatible with reactive refrigerants.
key_works: Weiß et al. (2025), “Stable Operation of Copper-Protected La(FeMnSi)13Hy Regenerators in a Magnetic Cooling Unit,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsaenm.4c00747).

title: Suppressing hydrogen-driven Curie-temperature drift
open: Prevent hydrogen redistribution and phase splitting in partially hydrogenated La(Fe,Si)13 during storage and cycling, predicting Curie-temperature drift from microstructure and chemical potentials.
status: The phenomenon has been studied for years, including a 2019 mechanistic analysis. Broad-history stability remains composition-dependent.
why: Preserves designed regenerator temperature profiles.
key_works: Fujita (2019), “Influence of electronic and metallographic structures on hydrogen redistribution in La(Fe,Si)13-based magnetocaloric compounds,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2019.03.006).

title: Tenfold higher magnetocaloric power density at retained efficiency
open: Proposed moonshot: increase useful cooling per complete-system volume tenfold against a specified prototype while preserving temperature lift and coefficient of performance.
status: High-power-density development continued through 2025. Material entropy alone excludes the crucial volume and energy costs of magnets, pumps, valves, and exchangers.
why: Makes magnetic cooling competitive where space and weight dominate.
key_works: Czernuszewicz et al. (2025), “From the Discovery of the Giant Magnetocaloric Effect to the Development of High-Power-Density Systems,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.202500545).

title: Manufacturable Curie-temperature gradients
open: Produce multilayer regenerators matching specified local transition temperatures despite batch variation, with robust tolerances for changing loads.
status: Layered regenerators are established. A 2025 analysis quantifies sensitivity to Curie-temperature uncertainty; consistent production remains a constraint.
why: Broadens cooling spans without wasting material or field.
key_works: Tomc et al. (2025), “Influence of Layering and Curie Temperature Uncertainty on the Performance of Multilayer Active Magnetic Regenerators,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202424282).

title: Abundant-element refrigerants for hydrogen liquefaction
open: Develop refrigerant sequences covering approximately 20–77 K that match rare-earth benchmarks under identical cyclic conditions, retaining properties after shaping and environmental exposure.
