status: Heavy-rare-earth compounds provide benchmarks. A 2025 FeCl2 study reports strong low-cost response, leaving moisture sensitivity and complete temperature coverage unresolved.
why: Reduces material cost and supply constraints in liquefaction.
key_works: Liu et al. (2024), “A matter of performance & criticality: a review of rare-earth-based magnetocaloric intermetallic compounds for hydrogen liquefaction,” [arXiv:2405.01128](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01128); Liu et al. (2025), “Ultralow-Cost magnetocaloric compound for Cryogenic Cooling,” [arXiv:2510.20458](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20458).

title: Scalable net-efficient magnetocaloric hydrogen liquefaction
open: Demonstrate sustained liquefaction with independently measured electricity per kilogram including field generation, auxiliaries, pumping, and ortho–para conversion, then validate industrial scaling.
status: Active-magnetic-regenerator hydrogen liquefaction was demonstrated by 2025. Competitive integrated throughput, efficiency, reliability, and cost remain open.
why: Reduces the energy penalty of liquid-hydrogen transport.
key_works: Kamiya et al. (2025), “Hydrogen liquefaction by active magnetic regenerative refrigeration,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cryogenics.2025.104205).

title: Net advantage of combined magnetic and mechanical caloric cycles
open: Establish when field-and-stress sequences reduce total losses after actuator work, friction, leakage, and fatigue, demonstrating repeatable cooling with complete energy accounting.
status: A second stimulus was shown to exploit hysteresis in 2018. Material reversibility does not establish a superior refrigerator.
why: Tests whether multicaloric control overcomes practical transition losses.
key_works: Gottschall et al. (2018), “A multicaloric cooling cycle that exploits thermal hysteresis,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0166-6).

title: Interlaboratory cyclic magnetocaloric benchmarks
open: Compare direct temperature changes, entropy, heat capacity, hysteresis, and delivered cooling under identical cycles with raw traces and uncertainty budgets.
status: A 2026 self-thermometry study achieved close agreement for one first-order material. General agreement across materials and frequencies remains open.
why: Prevents selection using incomparable single-sweep metrics.
key_works: Bastos et al. (2026), “Self-thermometry measurements of the adiabatic temperature change in first-order phase transition magnetocaloric materials,” [arXiv:2603.25429](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.25429).

title: Large reversible magnetic strain in robust polycrystals
open: Combine substantial field-driven twin-boundary motion, tensile toughness, and repeatable work in economical Ni–Mn polycrystals under realistic component constraints.
status: Single crystals show large strains; textured, porous, and toughened polycrystals improve selected properties. Grain constraints and fracture limit their simultaneous achievement.
why: Makes magnetic shape-memory actuation broadly manufacturable.
key_works: Ma et al. (2023), “Toughening of Ni-Mn-Based Polycrystalline Ferromagnetic Shape Memory Alloys,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma16165725).

title: Predictive fatigue limits for magnetic shape-memory microactuators
open: Predict effects of miniaturization, surface damage, mounting, and twin interactions on functional fatigue, demonstrating stable force and stroke across manufactured devices.
status: Bulk high-cycle studies date to at least 2010; small-scale fatigue was studied in 2024. Neither establishes general fabricated-device reliability.
why: Enables reliable microvalves and precision actuators.
key_works: Fareed et al. (2024), “Small-scale functional fatigue of a Ni-Mn-Ga Heusler alloy,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2024.119988); Aaltio et al. (2010), “High-cycle fatigue of 10M Ni-Mn-Ga magnetic shape memory alloy in reversed mechanical loading,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/0964-1726/19/7/075014).

title: Room-temperature single-molecule magnetic memory
open: Demonstrate a chemically identified molecule retaining a written magnetic state near 300 K for a specified useful time, excluding collective ordering and sweep-rate artifacts.
status: Pursued since the early 1990s. A dysprosium complex exhibited soft hysteresis up to 100 K in 2025; this does not establish long-term memory at that temperature.
why: Could enable molecular-scale information storage.
key_works: Emerson-King et al. (2025), “Soft magnetic hysteresis in a dysprosium amide–alkene complex up to 100 kelvin,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09138-0).

title: Predictive spin-relaxation rates across chemical families
open: Predict absolute relaxation times in unseen molecular crystals without fitting measured rates, quantifying electronic, phonon, anharmonic, and open-system errors.
status: Fourth-order ab initio master-equation methods achieved strong agreement in selected compounds in 2022. Transferability across chemistry remains incomplete.
why: Enables direct retention design instead of optimizing barrier height alone.
key_works: Lunghi (2022), “Toward exact predictions of spin-phonon relaxation times: An ab initio implementation of open quantum systems theory,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abn7880).

title: Chemical suppression of vibronic quantum tunneling
open: Identify vibrations and environments suppressing zero-field tunneling without opening faster thermal channels, then demonstrate chemically controlled rates matching microscopic models.
status: A 2024 nonperturbative treatment shows vibration effects even without thermally occupied modes. Reliable chemical design rules remain open.
why: Removes relaxation pathways untouched by high anisotropy barriers.
key_works: Mattioni et al. (2024), “Vibronic effects on the quantum tunnelling of magnetisation in Kramers single-molecule magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-44486-3).

title: Long coherence alongside long molecular magnetic retention
open: Engineer long population relaxation and coherent-superposition lifetimes together at elevated temperature, retaining useful control rates.
status: A 2025 microscopic calculation finds rapid dephasing despite slow magnetization relaxation in a high-blocking molecule. Overcoming this mismatch remains unresolved.
why: Determines whether better molecular magnets improve quantum processors.
key_works: Lunghi (2025), “Fourth-order quantum master equations reveal that spin-phonon decoherence undercuts long magnetization relaxation times in single-molecule magnets,” [arXiv:2507.20716](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20716).

title: Air-stable high-temperature single-molecule magnets
open: Combine high blocking with resistance to oxygen, moisture, desolvation, and processing while preserving the symmetry and vibrations responsible for slow relaxation.
status: Air-stable dysprosium macrocycles and exchange-bias tunneling suppression were demonstrated in 2024. Highest performance and convenient processing remain difficult together.
why: Makes practical packaging and manufacturing possible.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2024), “Record Quantum Tunneling Time in an Air-Stable Exchange-Bias Dysprosium Macrocycle,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c07412).

title: Preserving molecular magnetic performance on surfaces
open: Deposit high-performance molecules with controlled orientation while retaining bulk relaxation and hysteresis, separating decomposition, ligand-field changes, and substrate effects.
status: Surface-supported hysteresis exists. A 2024 assessment identifies retention of the best properties during deposition and contacting as unresolved.
why: Connects molecular synthesis to actual components.
key_works: Gabarró-Riera and Sañudo (2024), “Challenges for exploiting nanomagnet properties on surfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-024-01183-6).

title: Individually addressable dense molecular-magnet arrays
open: Write and read many identified molecules with quantified crosstalk, errors, retention, and yield without contacts or dipolar interactions destroying independent bistability.
status: Single-molecule measurements and surface organization supply components. Scalable addressing, wiring, and minimally disturbing readout remain unresolved.
why: Tests whether molecular dimensions yield usable storage density.
key_works: Gabarró-Riera and Sañudo (2024), “Challenges for exploiting nanomagnet properties on surfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-024-01183-6).

title: Reproducible microscopic origin of metal-free organic ferromagnetism
open: Establish predictive links between radicals, packing, exchange, and bulk room-temperature order using quantitative impurity accounting, element-sensitive probes, and independent replication.
status: Room-temperature organic ferromagnetism is reported. A 2025 study adds dichroism and microwave evidence in perylene-bisimide radicals; transferable synthesis rules remain open.
why: Establishes trustworthy foundations for lightweight organic magnets.
key_works: Yang et al. (2025), “Evidence of X-Ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism and Low-Field Microwave Absorption in Room-Temperature Organic Ferromagnetic Semiconductor,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/idm2.70002).

title: High-ordering-temperature molecular frameworks with useful magnetic strength
open: Increase magnetization and usable energy density while retaining high ordering temperature, coercivity, processing stability, and controlled redox stoichiometry.
status: Chromium–pyrazine networks reached ordering temperatures up to 242 °C in 2020. Strength, durability, and processing remain distinct constraints.
why: Extends molecular magnets into useful bulk functions.
key_works: Perlepe et al. (2020), “Metal-organic magnets with large coercivity and ordering temperatures up to 242°C,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb3861).

title: Fatigue-resistant optical switching of molecular magnetic bistability
open: Reversibly modify organized molecular magnetic bistability over many optical cycles without photochemical damage, establishing retained states and absorbed energy per operation.
status: A 2025 two-dimensional framework demonstrated coercivity photomodulation. Complete write–retain–erase operation and dense addressing remain open.
why: Enables contact-free reconfiguration of molecular magnets.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), “Two-Dimensional Metal–Organic Framework with High-Performance Single-Molecule Magnets as Nodes Showing Magnetic Coercivity Photomodulation,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c03704).

title: Early fault detection throughout long HTS windings
open: Locate any developing resistive region before damage despite pickup, current redistribution, and inaccessible cable interiors, with validated missed-event and false-alarm rates.
status: Slow normal-zone propagation has complicated protection for decades. Termination-based current-redistribution monitoring was demonstrated in fusion cables in 2022.
why: Protects costly magnets without excessive operating-current margins.
key_works: Teyber et al. (2022), “Current distribution monitoring enables quench and damage detection in superconducting fusion magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-26592-2).

title: Damage-free protection of large-energy REBCO magnets
open: Protect full-scale magnets against credible supply, joint, cooling, and local-conductor failures without excessive temperature, voltage, or stress, validating coupled models.
status: SPARC’s model-coil program demonstrated approximately 20 T at large scale and deliberate quench tests. Nonuniform dissipation and coupled failures remain central protection problems.
why: Makes compact fusion and large HTS installations maintainable.
key_works: Hartwig et al. (2024), “The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613); Pardo et al. (2025), “Screening currents increase thermal quench propagation speed in ultra-high-field REBCO magnets,” [arXiv:2509.06621](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06621).

title: Preventing REBCO delamination under combined cyclic loads
open: Prevent irreversible tape delamination under simultaneous transverse stress, bending, Lorentz forces, and thermal cycling, with statistically defensible production-length lifetimes.
status: A longstanding high-field constraint. A 2025 nested-coil study observed delamination following transitions below design current.
why: Converts intrinsic critical current into dependable operating field.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), “Observation of REBCO delamination in the resistive insulation nested coils,” [arXiv:2512.16647](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16647).

title: Reactor-lifetime REBCO under fusion neutron exposure
open: Predict critical current and mechanical integrity over reactor fluence under combined operating temperature, field, stress, and maintenance anneals.
status: In-situ cryogenic fusion-spectrum irradiation was reported in 2026. Combined-exposure lifetime extrapolation remains the stronger target.
why: Determines shielding, replacement schedules, and fusion power density.
key_works: Adams et al. (2026), “The performance of REBCO coated conductor during in situ cryogenic irradiation with fusion-spectrum neutrons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ae4548).

title: Repeatedly demountable high-current fusion joints
open: Qualify remotely separable and reusable joints retaining low resistance, current uniformity, integrity, and acceptable cryogenic heat under realistic contamination and alignment errors.
status: Demountable magnets were central to the 2015 ARC design, and low-resistance joints have advanced. Reactor lifecycle qualification remains open.
why: Enables internal-component replacement without discarding the magnet system.
key_works: Sorbom et al. (2015), “ARC: A compact, high-field, fusion nuclear science facility and demonstration power plant with demountable magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.008).

title: Tenfold cheaper qualified REBCO conductor
open: Proposed moonshot: reduce delivered cost per usable current–length tenfold at specified field, temperature, stress, and yield, including stabilization, inspection, rejects, and lifetime.
status: Long conductors and large magnets exist. Manufacturing cost and application-specific qualification still constrain deployment.
why: Broadens fusion, industrial, and research access to superconducting magnets.
key_works: Coombs et al. (2024), “High-temperature superconductors and their large-scale applications,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44287-024-00112-y).

title: Reliable 40 T-class all-superconducting user magnets
open: Deliver approximately 40 T with a useful bore, stable field, manageable stress, safe repeated cycles, and demonstrated facility availability.
status: The 2019 45.5 T result combined an HTS insert with a resistive background. All-superconducting systems have advanced into the 30 T range; 40 T development retains insulation and mechanical challenges.
why: Provides sustained extreme fields with lower electrical demand.
key_works: Hahn et al. (2019), “45.5-tesla direct-current magnetic field generated with a high-temperature superconducting magnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1293-1); Lu et al. (2025), “Observation of REBCO delamination in the resistive insulation nested coils,” [arXiv:2512.16647](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16647).

title: Accelerator-quality dipoles above 20 T
open: Build long reproducible dipoles exceeding 20 T with beam-quality harmonics, useful aperture, safe energy extraction, and economical series manufacture.
status: A 2019 roadmap specifies the coupled REBCO requirements. High-field conductors and short coils do not establish collider-ready long dipoles.
why: Increases collider energy within a fixed tunnel.
key_works: Wang, Gourlay, and Prestemon (2019), “Dipole Magnets above 20 Tesla: Research Needs for a Path via High-Temperature Superconducting REBCO Conductors,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3390/instruments3040062).

title: Predictable screening-current field errors in HTS magnets
open: Predict and suppress spatial errors and long-term drift from screening currents across ramps, thermal histories, and deformation without compromising current density or protection.
status: Simulations, conditioning, and conductor modifications provide partial control. Coupled field quality, force, and hysteretic history remain significant.
why: Enables stable NMR, imaging, and accelerator fields.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2023), “Review of progress and challenges of key mechanical issues in high-field superconducting magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwad001).

title: Persistent REBCO joints at full precision-magnet scale
open: Produce repeatable superconducting joints meeting current, field-angle, cycling, drift, yield, and repair requirements throughout a complete high-field persistent magnet.
status: A persistent 400 MHz NMR prototype with HTS joints was demonstrated in 2021. Scaling joint performance to more demanding complete systems remains open.
why: Reduces power-supply dependence and long-term field drift.
key_works: Yanagisawa et al. (2021), “Development of a persistent-mode NMR magnet with superconducting joints between high-temperature superconductors,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ac2120); Takeda et al. (2025), “Temperature, magnetic field, and field angular dependence of critical current of REBCO intermediate grown superconducting joint,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ae1eaa).

title: Training-free full-size Nb3Sn magnets throughout service life
open: Eliminate commissioning and retraining quenches while retaining field and integrity after thermal and irradiation cycles, establishing transferable support and impregnation methods.
status: Training persists after decades. A 2025 report describes nearly eliminated training in specific undulators; full-size collider qualification remains distinct.
why: Reduces commissioning time, helium use, and damage risk.
key_works: Barzi (2025), “Elimination of training in Nb3Sn and NbTi superconducting magnets,” [NAPAC2025 contribution](https://indico.jacow.org/event/97/contributions/10539/).

title: Uniform overpressure processing of large Bi-2212 coils
open: Reproduce high current throughout large complex windings while controlling bubbles, oxygen activity, dimensional changes, insulation compatibility, and temperature uniformity.
status: Overpressure processing enabled high-current round wire in 2014 and subsequent accelerator coils. Large-coil production yield remains difficult.
why: Provides an isotropic round-wire HTS route to powerful magnets.
key_works: Larbalestier et al. (2014), “Isotropic round-wire multifilament cuprate superconductor for generation of magnetic fields above 30 T,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3887).

title: Rapid-ramping HTS magnets with acceptable total losses
open: Achieve useful high-field ramp rates within total hysteretic, coupling, eddy-current, and refrigeration budgets while retaining field quality and protection.
status: Large static HTS magnets and rotating-machine applications exist. High static critical current does not establish efficient rapid-cycle operation.
why: Supports compact synchrotrons and responsive industrial magnets.
key_works: Coombs et al. (2024), “High-temperature superconductors and their large-scale applications,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44287-024-00112-y).

title: Practical ultrahigh-field whole-body MRI magnets
open: Reduce size, cryogenic burden, vibration sensitivity, and service complexity while retaining bore, homogeneity, stability, and fringe-field control under realistic imaging.
status: Human brain imaging at 11.7 T was demonstrated in 2024 with Iseult’s 132-ton magnet. Affordable reproducible installation remains unresolved.
why: Extends ultrahigh-field imaging beyond specialized installations.
key_works: Boulant et al. (2024), “In vivo imaging of the human brain with the Iseult 11.7-T MRI scanner,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-024-02472-7).

title: High-duty-cycle nondestructive 100 T-class pulsed magnets
open: Increase pulse count and useful duration near 100 T while extending fatigue life and reducing cooldown, vibration, and measurement noise.
status: Nondestructive 100 T-class pulses have existed since 2012. Peak field, pulse duration, repetition, and coil life remain conflicting objectives.
why: Makes extreme-field phase diagrams and weak signals more accessible.
key_works: National High Magnetic Field Laboratory (2021), “New Pulsed Magnet Reveals a New State of Matter in Kondo Insulator,” [laboratory report](https://nationalmaglab.org/news-events/news/75-tesla-duplex-magnet-kondo-insulator/).

title: Sustainable procurement for specialty superconducting wire
open: Establish purchasing, qualification, and funding mechanisms preserving specialized wire production, technical capability, supplier diversity, and research-scale access between major projects.
status: A 2023 stakeholder report proposes stewardship models addressing irregular demand. Durable implementation and evaluation across project cycles remain open.
why: Prevents manufacturing knowledge loss and future magnet bottlenecks.
key_works: Cooley, Amm, Hischier, Rotkoff, and Larbalestier (2023), “Business models to assure availability of advanced superconductors for the accelerator sector and promote stewardship of superconducting magnet technology for the US economy,” [arXiv:2308.03808](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03808).
